name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Democratic candidate David Crowley campaigns in Beloit with Maryland Gov. Wes Moore
description: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore came to Wisconsin looking for some company.  Moore, the first Black governor of Maryland and the only Black governor currently serving in office, traveled to Wisconsin on Friday to campaign with Democratic gubernatorial candidate and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley. The two made campaign stops in Beloit, Racine, Kenosha and M[...]
text:
Moore and Crowley hug before he takes the stage. Moore said after Evers introduced him to Crowley, “We just struck up a quick and early friendship.” (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Maryland Gov. Wes Moore came to Wisconsin looking for some company. 
Moore, the first Black governor of Maryland and the only Black governor currently serving in office, traveled to Wisconsin on Friday to campaign with Democratic gubernatorial candidate and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley. The two made campaign stops in Beloit, Racine, Kenosha and Milwaukee.
If elected, Crowley will be the first Black governor of Wisconsin. Moore told a group of about 120 gathered in a room in New Zion Baptist Church in Beloit that they have the opportunity to make history. However, he also said that’s not the reason Crowley should be elected.
“David understands that making history is not the assignment,” Moore said. “Making child poverty history is… Making history is not the assignment. Making pathways to work, wages and wealth for all of our citizens, and not just some, is. Making history is not the assignment. Getting this dark money out of politics — it is.”
Moore, who is only the third Black governor elected in U.S. history and a former U.S. Army  captain and paratrooper with the 82nd airborne division, came to Wisconsin riding a wave of popularity. Polls show he is leading his Republican opponent by nearly 30 points in his own reelection campaign. That’s, a different reality than in Wisconsin where Crowley is maintaining a slight lead over Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany by a margin in the low single digits. 
The crowd that gathered in Beloit to hear from Crowley and Moore was excited. One woman wore a colorful shirt with President Barack Obama’s face on it and was excited about getting her picture taken with both Moore and Crowley. Obama endorsed Cowley just the day before Moore’s visit. 
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore takes photos with Wisconsinites after urging them to vote for David Crowley in November. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Beloit is the home of Diane Hendricks, one of three billionaires contributing millions of dollars  to try to elect Crowley’s Republican opponent, Tom Tiffany.
During his Beloit campaign stop, Crowley criticized the amount of money being spent in the election, saying it could be used to help fund public schools, ensure childcare is affordable and expand Badgecare.
“All that money we’re seeing being spent and dumped into these elections. We could be solving the very issues that we’re talking about,” Crowley said. 
Crowley told reporters that having Moore campaigning with him would “help get us over the finish line and bring more people into the fold.” There are three weeks left until Election Day. 
New Zion Baptist Church Pastor James M. Ivy told the Examiner that the church was happy to open its doors for Crowley and Moore, believing that Crowley will be “what’s best for our city” and “what’s best for our state.”
Ivy said Crowley has impressed him as a candidate because he is “very connected to our story” and “not backed up by billionaires,” noting his support for people who are struggling including policies to improve access to jobs and housing and address homelessness.
At the end of the rally, Ivy told the crowd that they need to do everything they can to help get Crowley elected. 
“All that money we’re seeing being spent and dumped into these elections. We could be solving the very issues that we’re talking about,” Crowley said. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Moore told reporters that Crowley is “the right candidate for the right moment” and that’s why he wanted to travel to the Midwest to help. 
“I believe in David Crowley,” he told the crowd, “I respect people who are public servants who understand that public service is not for private gain. I respect people who understand that public service is about what are you going to do to be the legacy for those who will come after you… We have seen how David has risen to the occasion time after time. We have seen that he is willing to fight for families like yours and families like mine time after time. We have seen that he has never compromised his values, that he is willing to take on anybody, that he understands.”
Moore told attendees that he couldn’t “stress enough” the importance of who the governor is, especially given the current occupant of the White House. He said that “who you have in that statehouse matters” when there is an “overreaching and unchecked federal executive.” He noted that governors play a role in many significant decisions, including certifying elections and signing state budgets. 
Of Tiffany, Moore said that people have watched him “cosign on some of the most destructive policies” and vote for President Donald Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” which included deep cuts to healthcare as well as supporting Trump’s war in Iran. 
Quoting Maya Angelou, Moore said, “When someone shows you who they are, believe them.” The crowd repeated the phrase. “Here’s what I know, and here’s what I believe, Wisconsin,” he added, “you cannot send Tom Tiffany to the governor’s mansion.” 
Moore told reporters that he has known Crowley for a few years and was introduced to him by outgoing Gov. Tony Evers during Evers’ first term. Evers became a mentor of Moore’s when he was first elected, he said. 
Moore said after Evers introduced him to Crowley, “We just struck up a quick and early friendship.”
“We’ve had a lot of conversations about, not just the race, but also about a transition — how do you think about governance,” Moore said. 
“This stuff happens fast,” Moore said, adding that he thinks Crowley is uniquely prepared given his experience as the Milwaukee County executive. “These are serious times. These are times when we are watching a federal administration that has systematically attacked the relationship between the federal government and the states. … David is walking into this with a very sober understanding of what awaits, but also with a very optimistic view as to what can get done in this moment.”
During his second term in office, Trump has been in conflict with Democratic governors, including last week with Moore. Trump traveled to Baltimore to announce a multibillion dollar submarine manufacturing investment and requested that Moore be removed from the event’s speaking list, even though Moore helped negotiate and secure the deal.
Moore said that in dealing with the Trump administration, he is focused on protecting his constituents. 
“I’m a soldier by nature, and I’m a soldier by training. That’s what I do. While I will work with anybody — and this is the advice that I would give to David as well — I will bow to nobody,” More said. “Whenever the president or anybody thinks that a prerequisite of our relationship is being subservient to them, they will learn from me, they got another think coming.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: A beginner’s guide to the strange stories swirling around U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas
description: Welcome, newcomer, to the bewildering phantasmagoria of Kansas politics! Perhaps you hail from another state and have been told by election forecasters, political pundits or your great-aunt Sally that Kansas’ U.S. Senate race has become unexpectedly competitive. Perhaps you’re a Kansan who smartly ignores politics most of the time . Perhaps you’re — like me[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican , appears Sept. 12, 2026, at the Kansas State Fair debate. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)Welcome, newcomer, to the bewildering phantasmagoria of Kansas politics!
Perhaps you hail from another state and have been told by election forecasters, political pundits or your great-aunt Sally that Kansas’ U.S. Senate race has become unexpectedly competitive. Perhaps you’re a Kansan who smartly ignores politics most of the time . Perhaps you’re — like me — a masochist for political gossip.
Whoever you are, and wherever you come from, just know that U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas has a habit of stumbling into excruciatingly embarrassing news stories. National commentators repeatedly voice surprise at seeing Marshall in trouble.
Those of us following him in Kansas aren’t surprised.
Here’s a sampling of headlines from the past six years — from Marshall’s first campaign for Senate to the present — showing how deeply strange stories swarm around the former doctor. Yes, Democrat Adam Hamilton has his own issues (and Kansas Reflector has covered them at length). But he’s nothing compared to Marshall.
Unless otherwise specified, these stories come from Kansas Reflector. I’ve included links to each one so you can easily click through if you have questions. Enjoy this trip into the peculiar past and confounding psyche of Roger Marshall.
Roger Marshall was convicted of reckless driving in 2008. Here’s how it was erased (Jonathan Shorman and Bryan Lowry, Kansas City Star, June 21, 2020)
Ah, the urtext of Marshall deep dives. Do the same rules apply to Marshall as the rest of us? Apparently not, as a district court judge transformed the “suspended jail sentence for the future Kansas Congressman and Republican U.S. Senate candidate into a slap on the wrist.” Was the prosecutor in the case “also the son of Marshall’s business partner and neighbor”? Yup!
Senator Roger Marshall acknowledges Biden victory after objecting to electoral votes (Travis Meier, Fox 4 Kansas City, Jan. 7, 2021)
Just after arriving in the Senate, Marshall voted to reject Joe Biden’s certification as the next president. An attempted insurrection followed, but that didn’t change Marshall’s mind. When the Senate reconvened, he still voted against the results — supporting those who would foil the peaceful transfer of power. He made sure to issue a statement saying he disagreed, though.
U.S. Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., is shown on a monitor as Dr. Anthony Fauci (left) testifies before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on July 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
‘What a moron. Jesus Christ,’ Fauci mutters after terse exchange with Sen. Roger Marshall (Ariana Figueroa, Jan. 11, 2022)
That would be White House chief medical adviser Anthony Fauci. His words echo down through the years.
Marshall demands special parental warnings on television shows exploring gender issues (Tim Carpenter, May 7, 2022)
Overthrowing the government would be A-OK with the good doctor, but not talking about transgender people on TV shows. We have to draw the line somewhere.
This architect of Kansas’ tax policy failure mocks our state. Leaders can’t ignore recent history. (Clay Wirestone, Nov. 21, 2022)
Art Laffer promoted supply-side economics, the fringe theory that undergirded former Gov. Sam Brownback’s tax “experiment.” Wonder of wonders, he turned up on Marshall’s “Ag Talk” YouTube show a few years ago. Somehow, the two didn’t find time to explore the Kansas budget disaster.
Marshall, Estes offer enthusiastic support for U.S. House impeachment inquiry of Biden (Tim Carpenter, Sept. 13, 2023)
Sigh. I would love to write at length about some of these stories, but the sheer, dogged dumbness depicted strains my imagination. Yes, Marshall wanted an impeachment investigation into former President Joe Biden. Because of course he would.
Roger Marshall calls Kansas cabin home. Official trips took him near $1.2M Florida house (Daniel Desrochers and Jonathan Shorman, Kansas City Star, Sept. 25, 2024)
We’ve reached the second big kahuna of Marshall investigations, this corker from the Star about Marshall’s devotion to a “much larger and more expensive house that includes a boat dock on a bayou and is only a short walk away from Sarasota Bay” in Florida. Wonder why online wags taunt the senator as a “Florida man“? This is why.
Kansas lecturer on leave after ‘inappropriate reference to violence’ during class (Anna Kaminski, Oct. 9, 2024)
Marshall pops up here calling for the firing of a KU lecturer who made an inappropriately violent comment in class. Because he’s tending to the vital business of Kansas!
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall points to DEI hiring policies as factor in crash of flight from Wichita (Tim Carpenter, Feb. 4, 2025)
“U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas asserted President Joe Biden’s attempts to improve diversity among air traffic controllers by rejecting white male applicants factored in the catastrophic midair collision of a passenger jet from Wichita and a military helicopter.”
Kansas senator’s rural town hall meeting swamped by people mad at Trump administration (Calen Moore, High Plains Public Radio, March 1, 2025)
This town hall began the downward spiral around which Marshall’s re-election campaign still spins. He fled the event early and — to my knowledge — hasn’t held an open town hall since. That’s 19 months! The scene suggested that even rural Kansans didn’t support the vituperative chaos of President Donald Trump’s second term.
Marshall says paid agitators swamped Kansas forum. If he proves it, I’ll eat a copy of Project 2025. (Clay Wirestone, March 5, 2025)
I wrote this column, and the headline says it best. I still haven’t taken the smallest nibble.
Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas describes, with signage, the number of vaccines he claims U.S. children typically receive by age 18 during a Sept. 4, 2025, hearing of the U.S. Senate Finance Committee. (Kansas Reflector screen capture from U.S. Senate Finance Committee video)
RFK Jr., U.S. senator from Kansas find common ground on vaccines at contentious hearing (Anna Kaminski, Sept. 4, 2025)
As a former OB-GYN, Marshall might be expected to advocate for the health of newborns. Not when the ruddy face of RFK Jr. casts its spell! “By the time they’re 18 months, they’ve had 18 jabs,” Marshall proclaimed while the health secretary appeared before a Senate panel. “By the time they get to be old enough to vote, they have 76 jabs.”
U.S. Sen. Marshall of Kansas fears in-person town halls will lead to violence (Anna Kaminski, Sept. 29, 2025)
The headline says all you need to know. But this quote from Marshall perhaps explains why he’s struggling: “I’ve never seen such hatred coming out of people’s mouths at President Trump and his agenda. I don’t know why people are upset that the borders are safe and the price of gas and groceries are down and the economy’s looking better.”
Meet the Senate aide with a $44,000 taxpayer-funded commute (Daniel Lippman, Politico, Oct. 29, 2025)
“The top aide to Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas (Brent Robertson) charged $44,000 to taxpayers over the past two years in commuting expenses between Washington and Lynchburg, Virginia, where he lives, according to public records.”
‘Coordinated effort’: Kansas Republican leaders have a plan to cancel the 2026 U.S. Senate election (Clay Wirestone, June 19, 2026)
Here’s a crazy story nearly forgotten in the heat of campaign season. Marshall’s staff worked with Kansas legislative leaders on a law canceling the U.S. Senate election if he quit to work with the Trump administration. Legal experts suggested the move would be unconstitutional. But hey, Marshall tried overruling voters once already!
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas promises to refuse Trump administration appointment (Tim Carpenter, June 29, 2026)
Then “Meet the Press” asked Marshall about the law and he backtracked.
Marshall spent more time, taxpayer money near Florida property. It’s up for sale (Matthew Kelly, Kansas City Star, Aug. 24, 2026)
This important follow-up, also from the Star, reveals that “Marshall’s taxpayer-funded trips to the Sarasota area over three years were more extensive and more expensive than previously reported.” But he’s selling the Florida house now, so please don’t get mad at him.
A Doctor Sued 700 Patients for Debts; 81 Were Arrested. Now He’s a Senator. (Sarah Kliff, The New York Times, Sept. 9, 2026)
The recent pileup of bad Marshall news began with this story from the Gray Lady herself. Sure, it looks bad. Sure, it is bad. Contrary to what the doctor’s defenders say on social media, the arrests over unpaid bills weren’t inevitable: “Mr. Marshall’s lawyers repeatedly requested arrest warrants.”
The Rev. Adam Hamilton, a Democrat, and Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall appear on the debate stage on Sept. 12, 2026, at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector
Clamorous crowd dominates first Kansas U.S. Senate debate between Marshall, Hamilton (Anna Kaminski, Sept. 12, 2025)
“The scales of attendance at times tilted in Hamilton’s favor, as people booed, jeered and heckled Marshall’s answers.”
US Sen. Roger Marshall leaves paper trail in Florida while calling Kansas home (Anna Kaminski, Sept. 18, 2026)
Turns out that Marshall didn’t just own a home in Florida. He and his wife really lived there, applying for various licenses and sending paperwork from the Sarasota address. I’m sure it’s absolutely fine, though.
Senate aide’s side hustle raises questions (Daniel Lippman and Jacob Wendler, Politico, Oct. 7, 2026)
More Brent Robertson! This time, he reported “roughly $16,000 over the limit of what Senate staffers can make in outside income between 2021 to 2024.” The chief of staff’s lawyer said he was complying with ethics rules.
Roger Marshall’s complicated history of blurring the line between taxpayer dollars and campaign cash (Sherman Smith and Matt Fuller, Oct. 9, 2026)
This collaboration between the Reflector and MS NOW includes more startling revelations than you can shake a stick at, exposing the overlap between Marshall’s taxpayer-funded office and partisan political campaign. You hear a lot more about Robertson’s role in the senator’s office as well. Read it.
A Senator Facing Re-Election Settles a Bakery Bill, 6 Years Later (Tim Balk, The New York Times, Oct. 10, 2026)
Cookiegate! Or so it was dubbed by Hamilton’s campaign. We don’t need to hear any more about this, despite the repellant irony of a man who sued patients over unpaid medical debts stiffing a small-town bakery.
Marshall charged 18% on medical bills — more than other Kansas doctors who sued (Matthew Kelly, Kansas City Star, Oct. 11, 2026)
This latest dive into Marshall’s business practices arrived Sunday. Guess what? “The 18% annual interest rate Marshall applied to unpaid bills was by far the highest of the roughly 150 medical practices whose public records were reviewed by The Star.”
The incumbent surely yearns for Election Day, if only to end the pain.
As I wrote last month, none of this means Marshall will lose come Nov. 3. Republicans have money to burn and deep connections in the Sunflower State. The polling we’ve seen could be shaped by any number of confounding factors, such as conservative-leaning folks refusing to respond or Kansans wanting to send a message to Marshall.
You don’t have to be competent or even appealing to win elections as a GOP candidate in Kansas. Just look at former Gov. Sam Brownback (who for some reason endorsed Marshall on Saturday). He had all the charisma of pickled herring and kept winning elections.
Soon enough, Kansas Republican leaders will put Trump in the rearview mirror and pretend the past decade didn’t happen.
 
Kansas Reflector editor Sherman Smith and senior reporter Morgan Chilson appear at a Nov. 7, 2025, town hall in Hiawatha. (Photo by Jessica Tufts for Kansas Reflector)
We’ll still be here
National reporters and pundits have descended on Kansas. You can barely browse news websites without stumbling across another article titled “Why scarlet-crimson-ruby-red Kansas might vote for a — gasp — Democrat for the first time in 5,000 years.”
Here’s a lesson I learned over the course of a career that deposited me in two swing states: Florida and New Hampshire. (Yes, I worked in Florida back when it was a swing state.) Those national reporters will leave. Those Sunday talk shows will stop analyzing us. Steve Kornacki will forget all he ever knew about Johnson County.
We’ll still be here. The steadfast staff of Kansas Reflector live and work here, in Kansas. We care about the people who live here. And we will keep writing them and the policy that affects their lives, regardless of a single high-profile election.
I’m happy to welcome newcomers. But please, stick around. We’ll do the same.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Beckwith office initiates ex parte communication with judge
description: Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith’s office attempted to intervene in a criminal case involving a years-old hit-and-run but the reason is a mystery so far. The judge informed attorneys in the case and refused to consider the correspondence. “The Court finds that the correspondence constitutes an ex parte communication concerning a pending matter and is not […]
text:
Indiana Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith’s office, located inside the Statehouse, on June 27, 2025. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith’s office attempted to intervene in a criminal case involving a years-old hit-and-run but the reason is a mystery so far.
The judge informed attorneys in the case and refused to consider the correspondence.
“The Court finds that the correspondence constitutes an ex parte communication concerning a pending matter and is not appropriate for consideration by the Court pursuant to the Indiana Trial Rules,” reads a Sept. 25 order from Franklin Circuit Judge Alex Dudley, who is the special judge in Jordan Wadle’s Fayette County criminal case.
Ex parte communications are unauthorized because they don’t involve all legal parties in the case.
Beckwith’s office has not responded to multiple emails and phone calls from the Indiana Capital Chronicle starting Sept. 29.
The court confirmed the communication was a phone call, so there is no record to review.
The judge’s order came on the same day as a family member filed a handwritten emergency transport petition so Wadle could attend his father’s funeral on Sept. 26. The judge stroke the request and didn’t rule on it.
Larry Dale Wadle died Sept. 21 in Connersville. His obituary said he was a longtime deputy with the sheriff’s department and was Fayette County Sheriff from 1989 to 1991. He also was a pastor at East Side Pentecostal Church.
Beckwith is also a pastor.
Story continues below.
Wadle Order
 
According to an Indiana Supreme Court ruling, Wadle made unsolicited sexual advances toward a woman at a bar while drinking in 2015. There was an altercation in the parking lot with the woman’s husband and his brother, Charles Woodard.
“Although physically unprovoked by his interrogators, Wadle went on the offensive, punching and kicking. Wadle then returned to his car, suggesting an end to the fracas. But as Woodward retreated, Wadle’s car struck him from behind. Hell-bent on causing further injury, Wadle struck Woodward a second time, pinning him under a guardrail adjacent to the bar. Wadle then sped away, leaving his broken victim behind,” the ruling reads. “Police caught up with the suspected malefactor about an hour later just outside of town. Testing later revealed Wadle had a blood-alcohol level nearly twice the legal limit. Woodward ultimately survived the attack but spent nearly sixty days in the intensive care unit, having underwent surgery for a fractured skull and multiple broken ribs.”
A jury acquitted Wadle of aggravated battery in 2018 but found him guilty of four other charges: leaving the scene of an accident; operating a vehicle while intoxicated causing serious bodily injury; operating a vehicle while intoxicated endangering a person; and operating a vehicle while intoxicated with a blood-alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more.
Wadle received a 16-year sentence, with two suspended to probation.
His attorneys later challenged whether his multiple convictions in the case violated the doctrine of double jeopardy. The Indiana Supreme Court in 2020 agreed, adopting a new framework for double jeopardy and vacating all but one of his convictions: the level 3 felony for leaving the scene of an accident.
“And because this conviction alone justifies the penalty imposed, we further instruct the trial court to leave in place his sixteen-year sentence with two years suspended to probation,” the justices wrote.
Wadle in Nov. 2025 sought a modification of his sentence so he could be released and undergo testing to potentially donate a kidney to his father, who had end-stage renal disease. Dudley denied that request after a hearing.
His Wadle’s estimated release is Nov. 15.

title: Great Lakes lab hit by DOGE is hanging on — for now
description: If the Trump administration had its way, an Ann Arbor-based research lab that studies the Great Lakes and its coastal ecosystems would be gone.  So far, the Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory has survived the administration’s attempt to eliminate it entirely, and it’s continuing to operate with its federal funding largely intact thanks to members[...]
text:
The Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory in Ann Arbor, Mich., on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Robin Bravender/Michigan
Advance)If the Trump administration had its way, an Ann Arbor-based research lab that studies the Great Lakes and its coastal ecosystems would be gone. 
So far, the Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory has survived the administration’s attempt to eliminate it entirely, and it’s continuing to operate with its federal funding largely intact thanks to members of Congress who defied the White House’s wishes. 
But the lab is running at a fraction of its former capacity after early staff purges from the administration’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency effort aimed at squeezing the federal workforce. Former lab employees and allies of the research hub say the scaled-back organization is suffering from a loss of talent and institutional knowledge and is losing its ability to foresee disasters that could hurt the lakes and the communities that rely on them. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The science allows you to look forward, predict and anticipate problems and crises to help us get ahead of those,” said Deborah Lee, the former director of the Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory, or GLERL. Lee retired from her position in February 2025 as the DOGE operation was getting under way. 
Supporters of the lab say that scientific work is suffering after a wave of firings in early 2025, followed by voluntary departures from staffers who opted to accept the administration’s incentives for federal employees to retire early or resign.
“The big takeaway is that the laboratory has lost significant capacity in fundamental ecosystem research,” Lee said. “The second takeaway is that it has lost significant ability to communicate to the public the value of the science and to educate the public on the value of the science.” 
Deborah Lee (NOAA staff photo)
Lee, who had planned her retirement for about a year, was preparing for her farewell ceremony in late February 2025 when she received a list of employees that were to be fired by DOGE, she told Michigan Advance in a recent interview. 
“I was given 10 minutes to select one person off that list to not be fired,” Lee said. “That was all the input that I was permitted to have. I had no ability to identify who or shape the dismissals based on needs or efficiency.” 
The laboratory “went from 52 federal employees down to 34,” Lee said, noting that it put the lab at one fewer employee than it had when she started there a decade ago. 
The cuts included eight employees who were fired in February 2025 who were on “probationary” status, meaning they were new to their jobs or had been recently promoted, according to data compiled by AFGE 3908, a union that represents current and former laboratory staff. The administration targeted those positions, which have fewer protections, across the government as part of their early staff purge. 
By June 2025, the lab’s federal workforce was down about 35% from earlier that year, according to the union data. That included the probationary workers and others who retired or took administration incentives to leave their jobs. 
Targeted by Trump for closure
The Trump administration wants to eliminate the lab entirely. 
In its fiscal 2026 budget request to Congress, the White House sought to close NOAA’s GLERL locations in Ann Arbor and Muskegon. Trump’s fiscal 2027 budget request would also zero out the NOAA budget that funds GLERL. 
GLERL directed inquiries about its staffing and its work to Boulder, Colo.-based NOAA spokesperson Theo Stein, who said NOAA is “unable to address specific personnel questions” and declined to provide details about how many employees have left or about which, if any, were replaced. 
“The Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory continues to pursue its mission to conduct scientific research on the Great Lakes and coastal ecosystems, to create useful observations, data, models, and predictions to help manage water quality, ice cover, water levels, fisheries, and coastal safety, and to share that knowledge with decision-makers and the public,” Stein said. 
The Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory in Ann Arbor, Mich., on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Robin Bravender/MichiganAdvance)
Stein referred questions about the budget to the White House, which referred questions about the funding levels to NOAA and the White House Office of Management and Budget. OMB did not respond to a request for comment. This story will be updated when a response is received.
The Trump administration hasn’t gotten its wish to shutter the lab. 
“The zeroing out of the NOAA research budget that was proposed did not come to fruition,” said Gregory Dick, director of the Cooperative Institute of Great Lakes Research, which partners with the Great Lakes laboratory and co-locates its research arm at the GLERL site in Ann Arbor. Despite the administration’s proposed cuts, GLERL’s base funding “is close to flat, and so there haven’t been major cuts to the base funding for the NOAA lab,” Dick said. 
‘They’re stretched’
The Ann Arbor-based lab, launched in 1974, is one of seven NOAA research laboratories across the country. It’s the only one located in the Great Lakes region. Since its start, the lab’s research has included algal blooms caused by excess nutrients, the impact of climate change on the Great Lakes and invasive species. 
“It’s the only federal freshwater research laboratory that serves the Great Lakes, so what we’re working to do is to fully fund the work,” Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) told the Advance in an interview. “They’re working as hard as they can and they’re stretched.”
A member of NOAA monitors one of the Great Lakes buoys off the coast of Ludington. [Courtesy photo/Great Lakes Observing System]Dingell said she and other champions of the Great Lakes in Congress are trying to “make sure we get the funding and try to get it back to where it was when it was cut.” 
Next month’s midterm elections could tip the scales of power in Washington and shift priorities in Congress. “After this election, maybe we can get them back to their former level,” Dingell said of the lab. 
The laboratory has been without a permanent director since Lee’s retirement in early 2025. Jesse Feyen, the deputy director, is also performing the duties of the lab’s director. NOAA declined to comment on whether it plans to fill the role on a permanent basis. 
The lab’s communications team has also taken a hit. A pinned post on GLERL’s X account, dated Feb. 27, 2025, says: “Due to a reduction in staff, NOAA GLERL’s communications services will be taking an indefinite hiatus.” 
Nicole Rice, a longtime NOAA employee who had been promoted in GLERL’s communications shop, was among those probationary employees fired in 2025. 
“I was a 13-year continuous fed and I had been promoted due to some retirements,” Rice told the Advance in a recent interview. “But technically, my job title changed and they used that against me to say I was still in a probationary status.” She’s still fighting her termination with the Merit Systems Protection Board. 
Mark Zacharda, a local farmer, and Nicole Rice, a laid-off NOAA employee, discuss the impacts of federal government policies. Nov. 6, 2025. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
The lab lost its communications branch “in its entirety” and lost much of its ecosystem branch staff, Lee said. 
A reorganization of the laboratory merged its former ecosystem dynamics branch into another office. 
“Losing the ecosystems dynamic branch is probably one of the worst things that could happen,” Lee said. “That was where we produced all of our fundamental ecosystem research, and that research enabled us to develop state-of-the-art, state-of-the-science new forecasting products.”
That includes the laboratory’s harmful algal bloom forecast, which extends in three dimensions through the depths of the lake, she said. “If we had not been able to do the fundamental research in the laboratory that showed how that harmful algae moved up and down through the water column, and what caused it to form the thick scums on the surface, we wouldn’t have been able to produce a three-dimensional harmful algal bloom forecast.” 
The remaining staff in the lab has done a “really good job of finding ways” to get critical day-to-day activities done, said Dick. That includes going out into lakes and taking samples and measuring harmful toxins in the water to alert drinking water treatment plants. 
The cost of that “was a lot of the longer-term planning and really strategic research to prepare for the future,” he said. “To do the cutting-edge science that’s needed to develop the next generation of forecasts and products and scientific information that supports decision-making and supports the health and prosperity and safety of people on the Great Lakes.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Election workers prepare for early voting as talk of DOJ ‘intervention’ leaves advocates unsettled
description: CARTERSVILLE, Ga — In a warehouse in Bartow County, Georgia, election director Joseph Kirk stands in the middle of a long aisle of voting machines and starts performing his checks. It’s Tuesday, with only a week to go until the start of early voting. This year one of Georgia’s two U.S. Senate seats and all […]
text:
Georgia's ballot marking devices display the candidates and ballot questions for the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Election workers in Bartow County, Georgia conducted their pre-election tests of the voting equipment on Oct. 6, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderCARTERSVILLE, Ga — In a warehouse in Bartow County, Georgia, election director Joseph Kirk stands in the middle of a long aisle of voting machines and starts performing his checks.
It’s Tuesday, with only a week to go until the start of early voting. This year one of Georgia’s two U.S. Senate seats and all statewide offices are up for grabs. But before voters start casting their ballots, election officials across the state must conduct a sort of dress rehearsal, known as logic and accuracy testing, to ensure that all equipment is working properly. 
Joseph Kirk, the Bartow County elections director and past president of the Georgia Association of Voter Registration and Election Officials. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Kirk, who is also the past president of the Georgia Association of Voter Registration and Election Officials, said the routine testing procedure involves every piece of equipment and every procedure used during the voting process.
“We want to be sure that if there is a problem with how [the system] is collecting results, then we see that as part of the test, not afterwards as part of an audience,” Kirk said.
Common problems include screen malfunctions and other maintenance issues. But Kirk said during his time as election director, any discrepancy in tallying ballots they found during the testing have been the result of human error, not problems with the machines.
In addition to ensuring that voters have a smooth experience at the polls, Kirk said the process can help build trust in Georgia’s election system. Under state law, county administrators must publicly post the dates and times that testing will take place, and the public is invited to come and observe election workers while they perform the checks.
This is also likely the last major election to be conducted primarily on Georgia’s ballot-marking devices, which have been in place since 2020 and use a QR code to tally votes. The equipment has long faced criticism from activists who claim machines are less secure than paper ballots marked by hand, and state lawmakers are currently in the early stages of selecting Georgia’s next voting system.
Marilyn Marks, executive director of the advocacy group Coalition for Good Governance, has spent years speaking out against the machines and has repeatedly urged Georgia’s State Election Board to implement a switch to hand-marked ballots before the midterm elections. She worries that existing procedures don’t go far enough to protect voters against machines if they are tampered with.
“It is essential testing, don’t get me wrong; it is really necessary, but it can only catch a small number of issues,” she said. “It was never set up to be security testing to try to catch malware or anything. It is really just functional testing.”
Georgia election board leader requests federal ‘intervention’ in push for election system updates

But amid all her concerns about Georgia’s ballot-marking devices, she said recent actions from the State Election Board worry her more. Last week, the board’s executive director sent a letter to U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche requesting federal “intervention” ahead of the midterms. 
The Department of Justice did not respond to a request for comment.
Marks called the letter a “blank check,” to the Department of Justice and said she worries officials could be sent to monitor polling places or even seize voting machines.
“It is a license for chaos, and that is exactly what those board members were trying to do,” she said.
Congressional Democrats — including Georgia Reps. Sanford Bishop, Everton Blair, Hank Johnson and Nikema Williams — have also condemned Mills’ letter, labeling his actions “a clear attempt to sow public mistrust in the security of American elections.” They have also called on the State Election Board to publicly reassure Georgia residents that the state’s voting machines are secure and meet all federal requirements.
“Public confidence in elections depends in substantial part upon public officials communicating accurately, responsibly, and within the scope of their statutory authority — and without incompetently, or intentionally, mischaracterizing the law,” the letter states.
But those who are working on the ground to get voters out to the polls say there isn’t a clear consensus yet on how the State Election Board’s actions will impact voter turnout. Carmen Bergman of Greater Georgia, a group focused on registering and turning out conservative-leaning voters, said most Georgians she talked to were more concerned about issues like affordability and public safety than they were about election security.
“Among a group of election-focused individuals, yes, it is still very much on their minds,” Bergman said. “But any voter wants to feel confident that when they show up and cast their ballot, that it’s going to count and that it’s going to be cast securely.”
Mail-in voting is still an option for this year’s midterms. Here’s what voters should know.

Lauren Groh-Wargo, CEO of the left-leaning voting rights organization Fair Fight Action, also said she doesn’t think the State Election Board’s actions are influencing most voters. However, she said concerns about the reliability of absentee voting are having a tangible effect this year. According to the secretary of state’s office, only about 116,000 voters submitted absentee ballot requests this year, significantly fewer than the 285,000 voters who requested mail ballots during the last midterm elections in 2022.
“I think we are seeing real impacts of the lies and propaganda around issues with mail voting,” she said.
At this point, she added, her organization is focused on ensuring that voters have the information they need to cast their ballots.
“There’s fear mongering and voter suppression attempts going on to try to raise doubt, sow fear, sow distrust, so people stay home,” she said. “But the bottom line is, if our vote wasn’t powerful, they wouldn’t be wasting their time with all of these antics.”
Early voting for the midterm begins on Oct. 13. Voters can check their registration status, sample ballot and polling locations online through the secretary of state’s My Voter Page.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio US Senate candidates discuss how to fix Social Security
description: Candidates in Ohio’s tight U.S. Senate race briefly shared their plans to protect Social Security. With Social Security facing insolvency, tens of millions of retired Americans will face cuts to benefits in late 2032 unless Congress takes action first. Whoever wins the Ohio U.S. Senate race this year will be faced with big decisions over […]
text:
Former U.S. Senator Sherrod Brown, left, will take on U.S. Senator Jon Husted, right, in 2026. (Photos by CSPAN/Morgan Trau)Candidates in Ohio’s tight U.S. Senate race briefly shared their plans to protect Social Security. 
With Social Security facing insolvency, tens of millions of retired Americans will face cuts to benefits in late 2032 unless Congress takes action first. Whoever wins the Ohio U.S. Senate race this year will be faced with big decisions over the future of Social Security.
Only one of Ohio’s U.S. Senate candidates offered a specific fix. Experts say it’s popular, but by itself, inadequate.
The American Association of Retired Persons on Tuesday released its voter guide for the Nov. 3 midterm election. 
As part of it, the group published video of U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican, and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, answering questions about issues of importance.
Social Security ranks among them.
In June, the Social Security and Medicare Board of Trustees said that by 2032, the Social Security “fund’s reserves will become depleted and continuing program income will be sufficient to pay 78% of total scheduled benefits.”
The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimated that such a reduction would mean that more than 2 million Ohioans will lose an average of $487 a month, and cost the state $12.1 billion starting in 2032.
AARP Ohio reports that the program keeps more than 700,000 Ohio seniors out of poverty. With the average Social Security recipient in Ohio getting about $1,900 a month — or $23,000 a year — in benefits, the loss of a quarter of his or her income would leave a huge number destitute.
In his segment, Brown touted the Social Security Fairness Act, of which he was lead sponsor and which then-president Joe Biden signed into law just before he was forced from office in January 2025. The law ended prohibitions against 2.8 million Americans receiving Social Security benefits. 
“It restored full benefits to 250,000 Ohioans, including teachers, firefighters and police officers and other public employees,” Brown said, adding, “I’ll always oppose Wall Street’s efforts to privatize Social Security.”
That last statement was an apparent reference to President George W. Bush’s 2005 attempt to begin privatization of the benefit system. It turned out to be highly unpopular, and failed.
The law Brown championed was criticized by some because it further drained the trust fund and it added benefits mostly to workers with government pensions they paid into instead of Social Security.
Husted also expressed his commitment to protect Social Security, which he described as “a sacred promise to our seniors, and I am fully committed to protecting the benefits they have earned through a lifetime of hard work.”
As an example of that commitment, Husted said he “was proud to support the $6,000 tax deduction in the Working Family Tax Cut Act for seniors receiving Social Security.”
The Working Family Tax Cut Act is another name for President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. While it did provide the tax deduction Husted mentioned, it also provided $1 trillion in tax cuts to the richest 1% of Americans over 10 years.
The bill added an estimated $3.4 trillion to the federal deficit over the next 10 years. At the same time, it cut nearly $1 trillion from Medicaid over 10 years and it cut $186 billion from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP.
About 260,000 Ohio seniors were on Medicaid in 2025, and 256,000 on SNAP in 2022.
When it comes to what Ohio’s U.S. Senate candidates will do to make Social Security sound, Brown was the more specific.
“To ensure that Social Security benefits are there for future generations, we need to ensure that billionaires are paying their fair share by raising the tax cap so we can extend the life of the program,” he said.
It’s true that wage earners pay a 6.2% Social Security tax only on their first $184,000 of income, and that tax is matched by employers. So applying the tax all the way up the income scale will raise a lot more money.
A lot more, but not enough, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. 
Mark Goldwein, the group’s senior vice president, in June called the measure “raising the tax max” and called it “the most popular, most commonly discussed plan out there for raising revenue.” But, he told the Capital Journal, getting rid of the cap would close the solvency gap by only 50% and delay insolvency by 22 years if benefit rules stay the same.
Instead, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget advocates creating a bipartisan committee that would work quickly to come up with a variety of approaches to shore up Social Security long term. 
Measures could also include capping benefits for the wealthiest recipients, using a different system for cost-of-living adjustments and replacing employer Social Security and Medicare contributions with a flat tax on all compensation — including massive CEO pay and their gold-plated benefits.
That last proposal is projected to raise even more than raising the tax max as Brown proposed. Together, they appear to be more than sufficient to shore up the system.
For his part, Husted didn’t mention any specific fix.
“I stand ready to work with my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to work to ensure that Social Security remains strong and reliable for all Ohioans,” he said.
Asked what her group thinks should happen, AARP Ohio State Director Jenny Carlson said benefits need to be protected.
“AARP Ohio’s role is to make sure members of Congress understand that the solvency fight on Social Security is about money people have earned – and that they understand just how high the stakes are if Congress doesn’t deliver for the American people,” she said in an email.

title: Ohio voters will decide future of libraries with local ballot proposals this November
description: The November general election holds the future of some Ohio libraries in the balance,  just as it holds the future of candidates for statewide and legislative office. Voters across the state will see 16 libraries asking for local support, 11 of which will have renewal levies, two asking for renewals with an increase, and three […]
text:
The Gahanna branch of the Columbus Metropolitan Library.
(Photo by Susan Tebben/Ohio Capital Journal)The November general election holds the future of some Ohio libraries in the balance,  just as it holds the future of candidates for statewide and legislative office.
Voters across the state will see 16 libraries asking for local support, 11 of which will have renewal levies, two asking for renewals with an increase, and three with additional (new) levies, according to the Ohio Library Council.
“Depending on the library system, the levy may make up 40% of their revenue or more in some cases, so it’s very important and critical,” said Michelle Francis, executive director of the council.
The three library systems asking for additional help are Washington County Public Library with a 0.5-mill, 10-year measure; Toledo Lucas County Public Library with a three-mill, five-year levy, and Fairfield County’s Pickerington Public Library with a 1.5-mill continuing levy.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Stark County District Library is asking voters to renew its levy at an increased 2.3-mill, eight-year measure, up from the previous levy of 2 mills.
The Defiance Public Library wants to see approval of a 1.65-mill, 35-year levy, an increase of 0.9 mills from the levy the library says has been in place for more than two decades.
Asking for renewals are Ashland County’s Loudonville Public Library, Belmont County’s St. Clairsville Public Library and Barnesville Hutton Memorial Library, the Coshocton County District Library, Fulton County’s Swanton Public Library, the Guernsey County District Public Library, Hardin County’s Ada Public Library, Licking County’s Pataskala Public Library, Lorain County’s Herrick Memorial Library, Seneca County’s Bettsville Public Library, and the Wood County District Public Library.
Costs have gone up across the country, from the dinner table to the price of farm equipment, and libraries have not escaped that rise.
“It’s one of those things, and just like families, entities, and other organizations, libraries have been hit with inflationary costs as well,” Francis said.
Combined with reduced state funding through the Public Library Fund, keeping the lights on at a local library has relied more and more on local support.
In the last state operating budget, lawmakers in the Republican supermajority Ohio General Assembly changed the way the Public Library Fund appears in the budget, from a percentage of the General Revenue Fund to a lump-sum line item.
Advocates, including Francis and the Ohio Library Council, said changing the funding mechanism puts the fund at more risk for comprehensive cuts than it did when it was a percentage of the GRF.
The support necessary for local libraries includes a frequent talking point on Ohio’s campaign trail: property taxes.
Stark County’s library funding, for example, comes from 56% property taxes, according to the library’s own breakdown. The rest comes from mainly the state’s Public Library Fund (41%), along with investments (2%) and a combination of grants, donations, and fees (1%).
The library system said state funding has been reduced by $350,000 per year for it, while the cost of materials, salaries and staff benefits, along with security services, property insurance and vehicle repairs/maintenance have all “increased significantly.”
Failure to pass the levy would lead to reduced library hours, and a reduction in programs, services and materials, according to the Stark County system.
Public libraries remain popular among Ohioans, with a March 2026 poll conducted by Public Opinion Strategies showing 90% of voters polled found public libraries to be “important to the community.”
The support in the poll extended across partisan lines, with 83% of Republicans, 85% of independents, and 93% of Democrats saying they believed they get their money’s worth in services at their local libraries, based on the taxes paid to get them.
The support matches a national poll conducted by the Knight Foundation and the National Opinion Research Center at the University of Chicago, which in September found that 93% of Americans agree “budget cuts to their local public library would impact their community.”
The poll also found that 63% of Americans “view their local public library as an essential public service.”
Libraries have their roles as the election draws near as well. Local branches helped as voters met the Oct. 5 deadline for voter registration in the state, and systems like the Cincinnati & Hamilton County Public Library have collaborated with local organizations like the League of Women Voters, the ACLU, and the NAACP as the Greater Cincinnati Voter Collaborative to support voter participation.
“The library communicates with eligible voters through its branches, with digital resources, and through its legacy outreach program,” a profile on the American Library Association’s website stated of the library’s work in the collaborative.
The library association itself provides a voter engagement guide for libraries across the country to help increase voter turnout in each state.
“Voters trust their local libraries to provide accurate information about registration requirements, deadlines, locations, election dates, and ballot information,” said association president Dr. Maria McCauley.
“But libraries are more than voter education centers; they are civic connectors, places where people can interact with their neighbors and experience different perspectives.”

title: Ohio lawmakers introduce bills to add age limits, regulate electric bikes and electric scooters
description: Ohio Democratic lawmakers are introducing bills that would ban children 13 and younger from operating electric bikes and electric scooters, and require people wear helmets when riding e-bikes and e-scooters.  Ohio state Sen. Bill DeMora, D-Columbus, recently introduced Ohio Senate Bill 477 and Ohio state Rep. Eric Synenberg, D-Beachwood, is planning on intro[...]
text:
Electric bikes and electric scooters in Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal). Ohio Democratic lawmakers are introducing bills that would ban children 13 and younger from operating electric bikes and electric scooters, and require people wear helmets when riding e-bikes and e-scooters. 
Ohio state Sen. Bill DeMora, D-Columbus, recently introduced Ohio Senate Bill 477 and Ohio state Rep. Eric Synenberg, D-Beachwood, is planning on introducing his own bill in the coming weeks. 
“We are not trying to prevent Ohioans from using e-bikes and e-scooters,” Synenberg said. 
“Our goal is to make sure that riders understand the rules and risks before they ride, and give motorists, pedestrians, local government, law enforcement, and businesses clear and consistent expectations.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The bill would also ban riders younger than 18 from using high-powered e-bikes. Currently, Ohio law says a rider has to be at least 16 to rent a “low-speed micromobility device.” 
“These devices are not toys,” Synenberg said. 
“Unfortunately, not all of our kids are mature enough to have that kind of responsibility. We believe the state has an obligation to make sure all riders understand the risks before they get on these devices.”
Ohio organizes e-bikes by three classes. Class 1 and Class 2 e-bikes can go about 20 miles per hour with a mild pedal assist. 
Class 3 e-bikes can go up to 28 miles per hour with light pedaling. Riders must be at least 16 to operate a Class 3 e-bike and wear a helmet in Ohio. 
“Current law has no (age) limit for the Class 1 and Class 2 e-bikes,” Synenberg said. “A six-year-old could be riding one.” 
Children 11-14 made up nearly 40% of all pediatric injuries related to e-bikes and scooters nationwide, according to data from the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission. 
By mid-July, Akron Children’s Hospital surpassed the total number of e-bike and e-scooter injuries it treated in 2025, DeMora said. 
“These injuries include brain injuries, fractures, road rash, lung contusions, and injuries to major internal organs,” he said. 
“We’ve seen serious injuries and fatalities when e-bikes and e-scooters are struck by vehicles, including fatal crashes and hit and runs not only in metropolitan areas but in rural areas like Brown and Athens County.” 
A 58-year-old man riding an e-bike recently died from injuries he sustained after being hit by a van in Columbus.
The bills would set a 10 mile-per-hour limit on shared-use paths and five miles-per-hour limit on sidewalks. 
Personal e-bikes and e-scooters would also need to be registered with the state, which includes a $25 registration fee. Failure to register would result in a minor misdemeanor and the possibility of the vehicle being impounded for 30 days, Synenberg said. 
Several cities in Franklin County have their own regulations for e-bikes and e-scooters, but DeMora said that doesn’t go far enough. 
“It becomes increasingly difficult when every community has different rules, and riders may not know what requirements apply when they cross a line from one community to another,” he said.
The use of e-bikes and e-scooters will go down during winter months, but Synenberg said he wants to have these regulations in place by the spring. 
The Ohio lawmakers are currently on break and will come back after the November election. Any bill that does not pass before the two-year General Assembly ends in December would have to be reintroduced. 
“In lame duck, all things are possible,” DeMora said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: The mound next door: A celebration of the Ohio mound builders for Indigenous Peoples’ Day
description: When I enrolled at Ohio University in Athens, I had no idea that ancient burial mounds built by Indigenous peoples were next door to my college, in a nearby hamlet called The Plains. I graduated from Bellbrook High School, south of Dayton, in 2023, so I had grown up in Ohio, but I still knew […]
text:
Graphic from digital scroll-telling website produced by Ohio University class. When I enrolled at Ohio University in Athens, I had no idea that ancient burial mounds built by Indigenous peoples were next door to my college, in a nearby hamlet called The Plains.
 I graduated from Bellbrook High School, south of Dayton, in 2023, so I had grown up in Ohio, but I still knew very little about what was just beyond my college campus.
Many Ohioans recognize The Plains, an unincorporated community north of Athens, as the hometown of football star Joe Burrow, who graduated from Athens High School in 2015. It is also home to a much older part of Ohio’s history, dating back three millennia.
A college assignment to tell the story of the Adena Mounds in The Plains broadened my perspective about our past. We are surrounded by elements of Indigenous history and culture that can be easy to overlook.
The Adena culture was a prehistoric Native American civilization that flourished in the Ohio River Valley and surrounding regions from roughly 1,000 BCE to 200 CE.
Someone can drive through The Plains without realizing an earthwork is nearby. Students can spend four years at Ohio University without ever visiting one. I had been in the area without knowing much about what was there.
The mounds are not simply remnants of a distant past that exist only in photographs or history books. They are physical sites that remain part of the Ohio landscape, even as the areas around them have changed.

An eye-opening class assignment
“Immersive learning” is a favored phrase in higher education. In this case, I was part of a three-member team that spent six months studying nearby earthworks.
Our class visited the Adena earthworks in The Plains, primarily focusing on the Hartman Mound. We spent months researching the history of the earthworks, how they were constructed and what has happened to them over time.
The site once featured carefully planned burial mounds, earthen enclosures and ceremonial spaces. Excavations have revealed copper ornaments and pottery.
We also looked at other nearby mounds from a distance because they are on private property and are not always maintained or preserved in the same way. As we worked, it became clear just how easy these places are to miss.
For my colleagues, Ashim Faiaz Talukdar and Victor Morgan, and me, this six-month project was an opportunity to build skills in web design, photography, writing, fact-checking, graphics, animation and more. We submitted our work to the annual design challenge sponsored by the Society for News Design, or SND.
We wanted to document what is still there and give people a better understanding of the history and significance of these sites, including the differences in how nearby mounds have been preserved.
We created a form of digital storytelling called “scrollytelling.” The story unfolds as readers scroll through the page, allowing the research and visuals to guide them through the history of the mounds, their preservation and what could happen to them in the future.
Our “client” was a local support group, Friends of The Plains Mounds. We collaborated with the group’s president and subject-matter expert, Alex Armstrong, to help ensure accuracy and context.
Our title, “The Mound Next Door,” is not original. That phrase is also used by guides describing the Grave Creek Mound in Moundsville, West Virginia, a large Native American burial mound across the street from West Virginia Penitentiary.

Personal perspective
I am a college senior, on track to graduate in December.
As I grew up, America’s celebration of Columbus Day changed, prompting debate. In 2020, the City of Columbus designated October 12 as Indigenous Peoples’ Day. Some states recognize Indigenous Peoples’ Day, while Ohio does not.
As we reflect on Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples’ Day, the research project in The Plains feels especially relevant because it highlights a part of Ohio’s history that can be easy to overlook.
The earthworks are part of that history, and unlike something that exists only in a textbook, they can still be seen today.
On the second Monday in October, I’ll be thinking about the Indigenous earthworks near my college campus and “The Mound Next Door.” We should look a little closer at what has been here all along.
Kayla Payne is a senior at Ohio University’s School of Visual Communication, an active member of Alpha Gamma Delta, and serves on the chapter’s Executive Council as Director of Property.

 Catching Our Eye

• Sad. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Jo Ingles reports, “Libertarian candidate for Ohio governor makes shocking discovery while shooting ad.”
Libertarian candidate for Ohio governor Don Kissick made a disturbing discovery along the Maumee River near Toledo Thursday morning.
Kissick’s manager Steve Perkins said Kissick, along with Libertarian secretary of state candidate Tom Pruss, were making a campaign commercial.
“During that, a youth approached them and said hey, ‘I think this is a body in the river. Can you come see if this, back me up on this?’’” Perkins said in an interview. “And they went. And they looked, and it was.”
• Survivors and the Wexner name. WOSU’s Katie Geniusz reports, “Epstein, Strauss survivors call for Wexner’s name to be removed from Ohio State buildings.”
Survivors of Dr. Richard Strauss, the Ohio State team physician who sexually abused hundreds of victims, joined Jeffrey Epstein survivor Annie Farmer Thursday afternoon to call for Les Wexner’s name to be removed from Ohio State buildings. They appeared at a pop-up exhibit of the released Epstein files in Columbus.
The exhibit is named The Donald J. Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Reading Room, and has been displayed across the country. It shows the 3.5 million pages of the Epstein files the Department of Justice released in 2025 in 3,437 bound volumes. The exhibit is located at the Sanctuary on Neil, 618 Neil Ave., near Goodale Park, and is open until Oct. 11.
• Nuclear startup. Bloomberg reports, “Vivek Ramaswamy’s Nuclear Startup Raises at $1.9 Billion Value.”
Atlas Atomics, a nuclear startup cofounded and backed by Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, has raised capital at around $1.9 billion valuation, according to people familiar with the matter.
The series A fundraiser generated about $400 million in fresh money, the people said, declining to be identified because the information is private. General Catalyst is leading the round and Andreessen Horowitz is participating in the capital raise.
Atlas Atomics, General Catalyst and Andreessen Horowitz declined to comment.
• Eastern Gateway. In the Columbus Dispatch, Laura A. Bischoff and Jessie Balmert report, “Criminal charges filed in investigation of Ohio community college.”
Three former Eastern Gateway Community College employees, including the college’s last president, are accused of participating in a nearly $20 million scheme to divert federal Pell Grants and other financial aid from students, Ohio Auditor Keith Faber announced on Oct. 8.
Former President Michael Geoghegan and co-owners of the for-profit Student Resource Center, Michael Perik and Nicole Rowe Colclasure, were indicted on multiple felony charges, including engaging in a pattern of corrupt activity, for the alleged financial crimes. As a result, Eastern Gateway Community College closed in September 2025, eliminating a higher education option for students in eastern Ohio.
