title: Political polls historically underestimate Phil Scott. Will 2026 be different?
description:
Two new polls differ sharply on Vermont’s governor’s race. History suggests the numbers deserve a closer look.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Political polls historically underestimate Phil Scott. Will 2026 be different?.
text:
Gov. Phil Scott leaves the House of Representatives chamber after delivering his state of the state address at the Statehouse in Montpelier in January 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
In Vermont politics, late-summer polling has a habit of making Gov. Phil Scott look vulnerable — right up until election night proves he isn’t.
Two new September surveys appear to tell different stories about this year’s governor’s race. One, published by the University of New Hampshire, gives Democratic challenger Amanda Janoo a six-point lead, which falls in the survey’s margin of error. Another, by Vermont Public, puts Scott up by nine points 
Underneath that 15-point difference is a striking similarity. Both polls have Scott garnering almost exactly the same percentage of the vote.
UNH has him polling at 42%. Vermont Public has him at 43%. 
Despite the difference in margins, Harvard University government professor and polling expert Chase Harrison called the polls “very good” and “comparable.” 
The difference between the two polls appears among Janoo voters and those who remain undecided. UNH’s poll showed 6% of voters were undecided, while Vermont Public’s showed 20%. The Vermont Public poll seems more typical of a late-September survey, Harrison said, as voters have six weeks to make their decision.
Scott has a history of finishing considerably stronger than his autumn polling suggests. Since Scott first ran for governor in 2016, pre-election polls examined by VTDigger have placed his support at an average of about 14 percentage points below the share of the votes he ultimately received. His opponents, by comparison, have finished much closer to their polling numbers. 
That history raises the central question behind this year’s conflicting polls: Is Janoo actually making this the closest governor’s race Vermont has seen in years, or is Scott — the country’s most popular governor — once again entering October with support that polling has yet to capture?
Scott’s campaign spokesperson Emma Shouldice wrote in a statement last week that polling has “always undervalued” support for the Governor.
There is evidence for that argument, although the size of the gap has varied considerably from election to election.
The pattern dates to Scott’s first run for governor. An October 2016 Vermont Public poll showed Scott leading Democrat Sue Minter by just one point, with 14% of voters undecided. Scott won by nearly nine points, an eight-point wider margin than the poll suggested. 
The gap was negligible two years later, when Vermont Public had Scott 14 points ahead of Democrat Christine Hallquist and he won by nearly 15. It widened considerably after that. In 2020, Scott’s 32-point lead over David Zuckerman became a 41-point victory. Two years after that, UNH had Scott 17 points ahead of Democrat Brenda Siegel in September. He won by 47, a 30-point difference.
The pattern continued in the last gubernatorial election in 2024. UNH’s late-October poll that year had Scott 39 points ahead of Progressive Esther Charlestin. He won by nearly 52 points, about 13 more than the poll indicated. 
Past polling misses do not necessarily tell us what will happen this year. Pollsters say surveys measure voter opinion at a particular moment. They do not predict how undecided voters will break, who will turn out or how the electorate may change before election day.
UNH Survey Center director Andrew Smith and Vermont Public pollster Richard Clark told VTDigger in separate interviews that they were confident in the results of their polls.
When looking at the two surveys side-by-side, Harrison said it appears that when voters are “a little less undecided,” they opt for Janoo over Scott. That is different from what Vermont has seen in recent gubernatorial elections, when Scott has ultimately won by large margins.
“If Scott is seen as a competent incumbent, that can carry an awful lot of weight,” Harrison said. “If you’re seen as a competent incumbent who’s a member of an unpopular political party, you often see that weight — the weight of that incumbency — in people saying they don’t know or not turning out.”
So how can two reputable polls conducted at roughly the same time produce such different pictures of the same race?
One possibility is simply how the polls find and question voters.
Both used probability-based sampling, or randomized methods to select respondents from an entire population, rather than letting people opt in. Clark’s poll for Vermont Public uses a random sample of phone numbers. Respondents who don’t pick up phone calls are offered a text-to-web survey.
The UNH poll uses those techniques to recruit a panel of respondents who take repeated polls. Smith said UNH makes constant changes to the panel to reflect population changes. Respondents to this poll may be “slightly more engaged voters,” Harrison said.
The surveys also asked their gubernatorial questions differently.
Vermont Public’s gubernatorial election question came sixth in the survey, according to its methodology report, after questions about approval of President Donald Trump and Scott and how likely respondents were to vote in November.
UNH asked the question later, following a series of questions about voter likelihood.
Vermont Public’s respondents were “primed strongly to think of job performance,” whereas any such effect in the UNH poll would have been “much weaker,” Harrison said.
There may also be something different about the political environment this year. Negative partisanship is playing a significant role in the election, Smith said. The latest poll from NPR, PBS News and Marist found that 80% of Democrats say their vote for Congress is a vote against Trump.
“It’s not that you like your candidate so much, but you dislike the other party’s candidates more than you dislike your own,” Smith said. “The dynamics of this election, both with the way that midterm cycles work, with Trump’s unpopularity, the nationalization of it is what I think is going on, and why you’re seeing Democrats doing much better.”
That could matter particularly for Scott, a Republican who has repeatedly won broad support in heavily Democratic Vermont.
Pollsters nationally have struggled for years with underestimating Republican support. State-level misses in the 2016 presidential election led pollsters to reevaluate their weighting methods. Polling performed better in the 2018 midterms, but another round of misses in 2020 sent pollsters looking for additional explanations.
One might be that Republicans are less likely to participate in polls, Smith said. Pollsters sought to eliminate that bias in 2024 but were not entirely successful.
“Polling is not a statistical science; it’s a psychological science,” Smith said.
UNH and Vermont Public both weight their surveys using U.S. Census data, attempting to match respondent demographics to state-wide proportions for more accurate representation. UNH also uses previous presidential election data, a methodological difference Clark said could help explain the divergent results.
Whatever explains the difference between the two September polls, neither pollster thinks readers should treat his survey as a forecast of the November result.
Clark said pollsters “are not oracles,” and polling doesn’t claim to be predictive.
“I like to say in a poll it’s more like cutting with a chainsaw than cutting with a scalpel,” Clark said. “It is just not as precise as people would like to believe, but it’s also not as bad as people would like to believe.”
And there are reasons this year could break differently from Scott’s previous races. Clark said the race could be close with the result depending in part on voter turnout and enthusiasm for Janoo compared with voters motivated primarily by anger at Trump.
Age could matter, too. Older people tend to vote for Scott and head to the polls out of habit, Smith said. The question, he said, is whether “energized” young voters will show up as well.
That leaves the biggest question unresolved in both September polls: not where Scott’s support stands, but what happens to everyone else over the final weeks of the campaign.
So, what do polls mean? And why do they matter?
For social and political scientists, polls can provide insight into political preference. 
“I want to know if a vote for Phil Scott is connected to a vote for Becca Ballant, and who are the ones who are voting for both?”  Clark said. “We’ve asked questions about healthcare and the provision of healthcare, how that factors into one’s political preference.”
Clark said the public focus on the polling “horserace” can obscure what voters are actually deciding.
“We get so caught up in all of that we forget that we’re electing somebody to lead our state,” he said. “We’re electing somebody to represent us in Congress. That’s what really matters. Let’s talk about their opinion.”

title: At odds over the “Aud,” Vermont Coyotes announce departure from Barre
description:
This season will be their last at the Barre Civic Center, the team announced.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  At odds over the “Aud,” Vermont Coyotes announce departure from Barre.
text:
A practice session with the Vermont Coyotes basketball team. Photo courtesy of Vermont Coyotes

BARRE — A fist bump from a Vermont Frost Heaves player turned Anthony Marques into a fan who attended 102 of the team’s consecutive games. Years later, he brought a team of his own, the Vermont Coyotes, to Barre.
When he started the state’s only minor-league basketball team in 2024, it felt natural to bring them to Barre, said Brandy Marie, the team’s staff performance analyst. 
That made the Barre Civic Center, nicknamed the Auditorium or the “Aud,” their home court. 
Two years later, however, that connection has been severed. The Coyotes announced this month that this coming season will be the last one the team plays at the civic center. 
The Coyotes and the auditorium’s owner, the city of Barre, disagree on a key issue: the team’s use of the space outside of games and official practices. Officials from the team say they deserve flexibility to use the space beyond what’s laid out in the current contract. 
The Coyotes learned in their first season that “if you want to be a competitive professional basketball team, two practices a week didn’t really fit,” said Tiffany Mason, chief operation officer for the Coyotes. “We just wanted access when the gym wasn’t being used.” 
Officials from the city say they want to keep the auditorium as a public resource, and they can’t just hand over the keys. 
“You would love to have a facility that is yours,” said Barre city manager Patrick Cushing. “That’s not what the Aud is. The Aud is a community center that can support a team, or at least support the base of a team. Like, do they need practice elsewhere? Maybe. Like, that’s up to them.”
The Coyotes’ current contract provides them with a discounted rate of $50 per hour to use the court during games, plus complimentary practice time that adds up to about $4,000 per season, Cushing said. He claimed that with the “redlines,”or suggestions, the Coyotes made on the new contract, the team was asking the city to comp about $10,000 in court time per year. 
In addition, the team’s request for flexible use of the court was impractical because the city needed to know when people would be in the building. 
“The city is responsible through their insurance of who is in and on the property, so we need to at least know when they need to be there,” Cushing said. 
Mason said the team is providing the city with free marketing by promoting the court and the city on its platforms, along with partnering with local businesses and fundraising for local causes.
“Every time we post and feature the Barre Auditorium or feature businesses in Barre, we are providing that free of charge for the city, for the civic center, and we never asked for anything in return,” Mason said. 
Cushing said he hadn’t seen any hard numbers that show the team was bringing in more revenue for the city outside of its court rental. 
“I’m sure that there is some kind of influx during game nights, or I hope so at least,” he said. “I’m not sure the dollar amount that’s being brought in during their games, and I don’t think we have any data one way or the other. I don’t know how the Coyotes are, besides just saying it, getting that information.” 
Mason also pointed out what she sees as hypocrisy on the city’s part. The former city manager, Nick Storellicastro, was given access to the civic center for personal use. 
According to documents from a May 2025 city council meeting, Mayor Thom Lauzon allowed Storellicastro to use the civic center when it wasn’t otherwise occupied, although the letter stipulates the use must be “informal” and releases the city from any liability. Lauzon did not reply by publication time to a request for comment on the letter. 
Cushing said the city was still willing to come back to the table if the Coyotes were interested. But Mason said the team’s relationship with the city had already been too damaged by the situation. 
“The issue is more than a contract,” she said. “I think that how things were presented before the Coyotes came to the Aud is very different. That relationship is very different than what we thought we were entering, which we thought was a partnership.”
But the Coyotes haven’t started househunting for a new space yet. Marie said the focus right now was completely on the coming season, which begins with an away game against the Hartford Colts on Oct. 17. The team’s home opener isn’t until Dec. 5 as they await repairs on the civic center’s heating and air conditioning system.
“We want as many people as possible to pack the auditorium every home game, because we want to give Barre a fantastic bunch of games, and we really want to show what a benefit the Coyotes can be to the community,” Mason said.

title: South Dakota wildlife officials offer hunting license refunds as deer disease reports continue
description: Reports of deer deaths from a viral disease have spiked as hunters take to the fields in South Dakota, and state wildlife officials are reducing some hunting opportunities and offering hunting-license refunds to protect deer numbers. Epizootic hemorrhagic disease is a viral illness spread by tiny biting midges typically found along muddy shorelines. In South[...]
text:
A male white-tailed deer roams a field. South Dakota is adjusting deer-hunting policies as a disease affects deer populations. (Courtesy U.S. Department of Agriculture)Reports of deer deaths from a viral disease have spiked as hunters take to the fields in South Dakota, and state wildlife officials are reducing some hunting opportunities and offering hunting-license refunds to protect deer numbers.
Epizootic hemorrhagic disease is a viral illness spread by tiny biting midges typically found along muddy shorelines. In South Dakota, the disease primarily impacts white-tailed deer, according to Game, Fish and Parks Senior Wildlife Biologist Byron Buckley.
“Because white-tailed deer generally inhabit the areas where these midges currently are,” he told the Game, Fish and Parks Commission on Thursday in Pierre.
Mule deer, bighorn sheep, elk and pronghorn can also be infected. The department says the disease usually affects deer herds in late summer or early fall. Warm conditions can extend the period when the insects are active, while a hard freeze generally kills them off, bringing a seasonal outbreak to an end.
State commission replaces controversial wildlife predator bounty with new programs

Buckley said weather strongly influences outbreaks. This year’s outbreak started in July and continued as South Dakota experienced an unusually warm, dry September with some heavy rain.
Retired Game, Fish and Parks lead biologist George Vandel said those conditions — drier dry periods and wetter wet periods — can create the environment where midges thrive best: muddy areas that are sometimes covered by water and sometimes exposed to the air. 
During the commission’s monthly meeting, Buckley said the department now has about 407 reports this year of dead deer due to the illness: 376 suspected cases and 31-lab-confirmed. During the commission’s Sept. 10-11 meeting, the count was 196, he said. Though he said it’s not unusual for a spike in reports to come in during that timeframe. 
“So a lot of our reports have come from the month of October,” Buckley said. “Now, that could be because we are seeing the disease a lot more or that there’s just a lot more people on the landscape.” 
Waterfowl, grouse, dove and archery deer hunting seasons all began in September.  
The number of reported cases for 2026 is slightly higher than the total reported for all of 2025, according to the state’s EHD map, though Buckley described this year’s numbers as roughly comparable to the previous two years.
The state has taken several steps to limit deer hunting in outbreak-affected areas, aiming to give deer populations a better chance to recover. The department removed mentored and youth deer licenses in nine southeastern South Dakota counties where outbreaks have affected deer in the past two years. It also removed 62 unsold licenses, two in McPherson County and 60 in Dewey County. The state changed statewide archery license rules, which previously allowed hunters to take any deer, to buck-only licenses.
Buckley said the department is now offering a further option: Hunters holding deer licenses in 16 counties along the Missouri River corridor can voluntarily return their licenses for a full refund.
Wildlife Division Director Tom Kirschenmann said the department may add counties as more October reports arrive.
“We’re trying to be somewhat strategic about it, but we’re also trying to be proactive about where we offer this up,” Kirschenmann said.
The department asks people to report sick or dead deer via methods listed at gfp.sd.gov/contactus. Buckley said officials enter reports into a system that updates the department’s public online map.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Shad White blames Bennie Thompson for Delta woes. Is that fair?
description: State Rep. Robert Johnson, D-Natchez, and state Auditor Shad White exchange words after White’s criticism of U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson during a public redistricting hearing at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Based on state Auditor Shad White’s logic, it is time to clean house of all Republican and Democratic Mississippi politicians on both the state and federal level.
At a recent public hearing about legislative redistricting, the Republican White argued that Mississippi’s congressional map should be redrawn with the intention of removing U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson from office. White said Thompson has done a poor job representing the 2nd District, which stretches through the Delta, along the Mississippi River and into Jackson.
Since the April U.S. Supreme Court decision that erased protections for Black voting strength, many in Mississippi’s Republican leadership have called for redrawing the state’s four congressional districts to ensure the defeat of Thompson, the state’s only Black member of Congress.
White, who is expected to run for governor in 2027, has been particularly vocal in the call to unseat Thompson, also the state’s only Democratic congressional member. It has appeared Republican leaders wanted Thompson removed for solely partisan reasons.
But at the redistricting hearing, White said Thompson should be removed because he is not adequately representing his district, which includes the poverty-stricken Delta.
Placing blame for Delta on Bennie Thompson
“I travel all over this state, but I travel a ton in the Delta, too…,” White said at the redistricting hearing recently at the Mississippi Capitol. “The Delta has been at the bottom of far too many rankings for far too long, and the Delta deserves better leadership than Bennie Thompson. It just does. The Delta deserves a congressman who’s going to deliver.”
Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., talks during a hearing on Capitol Hill, Jan. 10, 2024, in Washington.  Credit: AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib
It should be pointed out that the Delta can vote for someone other than Thompson. Delta voters will have that opportunity in November when Republican Ron Eller challenges him. What White is most likely proposing is to split up the Delta’s Black population through redistricting.
Granted, Thompson, has been representing most of the Mississippi Delta for a long time – first elected in 1993. And, yes, the Mississippi Delta has more than its share of problems and has had those problems for generations.
But blaming all of the Delta’s problems on one U.S. House member – one of 435 – seems disingenuous.
Thompson’s 2nd District, which covers western Mississippi, is one of the nation’s poorest districts. It is ranked as having the sixth highest poverty rate at 25%, the website Overflow Data reported in July 2025, based on U.S. Census information.
Using Shad White’s logic, what about other politicians?
But all four Mississippi congressional districts have poverty rates significantly higher than the national average of 12.5%, according to the Coalition on Human Needs.
Are the state’s three Republican congressmen – Trent Kelly, Michael Guest and Mike Ezell – falling down on their jobs and also needing to be replaced, using White’s logic?
And what about the state’s two U.S. senators – Republicans Roger Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith – who are two of 100, giving them the opportunity to have much more influence than Thompson?
Why hasn’t Wicker, who has been in the Senate since 2007, and Hyde-Smith who has been in the Senate since 2018, had more of an impact on the 2nd District?
And don’t forget before Wicker and Hyde-Smith, Mississippi’s senators were Republicans Trent Lott, who was elected in 1988, and Thad Cochran, elected in 1978.
Cochran was chairman of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, and Lott was a former Senate majority leader.  With all that power, why couldn’t they fix the 2nd District?
And of course on the state level, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves has had two terms as governor and two as lieutenant governor – two of the most impactful policymaking posts in state government. And White’s old boss – Phil Bryant – served two terms as governor and one as lieutenant governor.
Couldn’t they fix the 2nd District – or for that matter the state?
Remember, Mississippi routinely has the first or second highest poverty rate.
The problems facing Mississippi, including the 2nd District, are complex. To think one politician can fix them all is fanciful, especially when the politician is one U.S. House member whose proposed fixes are consistently stymied by Mississippi’s Republican majority. 
Criticism of Trump makes Bennie Thompson a target
Perhaps the real reason Thompson is in the crosshairs of Mississippi’s  Republican leadership is that he is the state’s highest-profile critic of their party leader and often-times political benefactor – Republican President Donald Trump.
Thompson led the House committee that assigned a large part of the blame for the Jan. 6, 2021, attacks on the U.S. Capitol on Trump and cited him for being the first presidential candidate in U.S. history to attempt to overturn the results of a national election.
But perhaps it sounds a lot better for White to say Bennie Thompson is responsible for the poverty in the 2nd District than to say he should be replaced because he has been critical of President Trump.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont high schools feel the pinch with fewer international students enrolling
description:
Visa delays and shifting Trump administration policies are leading to less international interest in a U.S. education, school leaders say.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont high schools feel the pinch with fewer international students enrolling.
text:
St. Johnsbury Academy viewed from the north. Photo by Ascended Dreamer – CC BY 4.0.

International student enrollment at some Vermont high schools is down by about half after Trump administration policy changes, including a requirement that foreign students allow vetting of their social media accounts.
The decline in international students impacts the culture and bottom line at these schools, a number of them historic private academies that serve as de facto public high schools for the surrounding area in addition to taking on boarding students from around the country and world.
“All students benefit from the opportunity to develop empathy for others and to form friendships with peers from outside of their home community,” said Nora Dock, assistant head of school for enrollment and student experience at Vermont Academy in Saxtons River, in an email. “International education strengthens individual character just as much as it strengthens the US economy.”
St. Johnsbury Academy — one of those historic academies — enrolled 100 international students this year, according to Headmaster Sharon Howell, which accounts for 11% of the school’s total enrollment and 75% of its boarding population. This is down from 185 in 2024, when it boasted the highest number of international students for any public or private K-12 school in the state and the 33rd highest in the country, according to data from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Howell attributes the decline to shifting federal policies.
“In 2025-26, a pause on student visas prevented at least eight admitted students from enrolling, and we saw similar visa difficulties again this year,” she said in an email. “Changes in federal policy toward international students have created uncertainty for families abroad, and I believe that has made some of them hesitant to choose a U.S. school.”
The Trump administration temporarily froze all student visa interviews in May 2025 and, when they resumed a month later, required applicants to make all their social media accounts public for vetting. Since the change, student visa appointments have been scarce.
According to State Department data, the number of visas issued to all types of international students, including those in K-12, college, vocational and cultural exchange programs, dropped 35% in summer 2025 compared to the previous summer.
In Vermont, there were 1,438 international students studying at all levels in September 2026, according to the Department of Homeland Security — a 10% decline from 1,607 the prior year.
“International students have been part of St. Johnsbury Academy for a long time, and they are central to our identity and mission,” Howell said. “They bring a range of cultures, faiths and nationalities to our campus and to the Northeast Kingdom, and that exchange enriches the experience of every student here, local and international alike. We value it deeply.”
In Manchester, Burr & Burton Academy — another historic private academy — is also seeing a decline in international students. René Driscoll, director of international admissions, said the school typically had around 70 international students, about 10% of overall enrollment, before the COVID-19 pandemic and has a mere 35 enrolled this year, 6% of overall enrollment.
Driscoll said she is hearing that immigration policy and visa delays are impacting international families’ decision-making, including worries about a yet-to-be-implemented policy that could potentially restrict students’ time in the country.
This summer, the Department of Homeland Security announced that international students would be admitted to the country for a fixed period of time, not to exceed four years, instead of the duration of their academic program. Students needing additional time — or high schoolers wanting to transition to study at a U.S. college — would have to seek approval from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for an extension. 
In August, a coalition of higher education groups and unions sued the Trump administration to stop the change. A federal judge temporarily blocked the rule in mid-September, one day before its scheduled implementation, while that lawsuit advances. The Department of Homeland Security appealed the judge’s ruling last week.
If enforced, the “damage to the higher education system and to the economy of the United States is likely to be catastrophic,” wrote U.S. District Court Judge F. Dennis Saylor in his ruling, noting that many American colleges and universities are already struggling with declining enrollment based on demographic changes.
There are currently 1.6 million international students pursuing full-time academic or language training programs in the United States, Saylor wrote. His ruling also cited a study that found international students contributed $44 billion to the economy in 2023-2024.
According to Howell, the four-year rule “would present a significant challenge and would require some families to make difficult decisions about their children’s education.”
Driscoll said the changes in international student enrollment haven’t yet affected Burr & Burton’s budget or staffing, but the possibility is “certainly on (their) radar.” Current international student tuition for the school is $64,618 for a full year, while domestic private-pay tuition is $25,933. Tuition for local students for whom Burr & Burton is the de facto high school is paid through state property taxes.
International enrollment at Vermont high schools also appears to be declining for other reasons in addition to immigration policies. Danny O’Brien, head of school at The Putney School, said in an email that only 14% of their student body is international this year compared to a historical average of around 20%.
“The reasons we most often hear for the decline are that fewer students are seeing a U.S. college education as the ‘golden ticket’ to career success and advancement, and so are less likely to want to study here as a stepping stone,” O’Brien said.
The Putney School is seeing an especially stark decline in students coming from Asia, he said, where “there has been major domestic investment in ‘homegrown’ academic quality, availability, and resources.” Howell also noted a significant decline in students from China at St. Johnsbury Academy.
Dock, at Vermont Academy, said that the United States is “no longer a preferred destination, in part because of changes (perceived and otherwise) to the student visa process.”
Vermont Academy enrolled 90 international students in 2024, according to ICE data — the second-highest international student population at a high school in the state. International students typically account for 25% of the Academy’s total enrollment, Dock said.
She said this year’s international student enrollment remains within the school’s normal range, though a small number of admitted and enrolled new international students were not able to attend because their visas were declined, which she called “atypical.”
Vermont Academy is also hearing from its international education consultant partners that “more families are looking to Canada, Australia and other English-speaking destinations for their children,” Dock said.
“Last year we had two families from Western Europe withdraw their applications to schools in the U.S. because they did not like the political climate and wished to send their children somewhere more hospitable,” she added.
O’Brien said that the lower international enrollment has created some short-term budgetary pressures, which he said The Putney School has been planning for, but declined to discuss details.
“We are more concerned with the long-term implications of the U.S. being seen as distrustful and unwelcoming of its international students and the reputational damage to U.S. education,” he said. “These are perceptions that can take root quickly and have lasting effects.”
Lower birth rates mean fewer domestic boarding applicants nationally, he added, another reason international families matter to The Putney School.
An outlier to the trend, so far, is Lyndon Institute, another historic private academy. The school has seen a recent increase in international students, enrolling 24 last year and 31 this year, said Erik Oliver, vice president of external relations and advancement.
Oliver said the school is hearing more questions from families seeking to understand the recent federal rule changes, but they are not hearing that those concerns are discouraging students from applying. 
“We are hearing strong interest in the kind of high school experience Lyndon Institute offers: strong preparation for college combined with practical, hands-on learning, opportunities to explore new interests, and a supportive community where students are known and supported,” Oliver said. “That is reflected in the positive response we are seeing in our international enrollment.”
In spite of the uptick in international students this year, Lyndon Institute officials are mindful of the potential impact on enrollment and tuition revenue in the future.
At St. Johnsbury Academy, where the decline in international students has been steep, Headmaster Howell said the school is “on solid financial footing” and is “planning carefully so it is prepared for whatever comes.” Howell said she was not able to comment further on how exactly the Academy is responding financially to the decline.
“Above all, we remain committed to our international students and everything they bring to our community, and we hope to see policies that once again make the U.S. a welcoming destination for students from around the world,” she said.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: With MAGA friends like these, do Arkansas Republicans need enemies?
description: There are two predictions that I never could have made about Arkansas politics in 2026. One is that Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who has made culture war fights her calling card, would be accused by conservative influencers of going woke. The other is that Sen. Tom Cotton, a staunch defender of President Donald Trump’s […]
text:
Thousands of Nebraskans gather in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds for a midterms rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)There are two predictions that I never could have made about Arkansas politics in 2026.
One is that Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who has made culture war fights her calling card, would be accused by conservative influencers of going woke.
The other is that Sen. Tom Cotton, a staunch defender of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and war in Iran, would be doxxed by the president. Or that it would be sparked by a dispute over when to turn back your clocks.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The two most bizarre episodes of Arkansas’ midterm election campaign are a stark reminder of how much Trump and his allies have upended state politics. They also highlight how Trump and his base have gone from an asset to a headache for Arkansas Republicans.
Sanders’ now-infamous Brad ad featured an actor playing a Medicaid recipient sitting on a bean bag chair eating cheese balls and playing video games. It felt like the latest ragebait to elicit clicks and national coverage.
Arkansas voters know the playbook well. From executive orders banning “Latinx” to campaign ads mocking trans athletes, Sanders knows how to gin up outrage on the left. This time she hoped to do it while touting Arkansas’ Medicaid work requirements taking effect next year.
But the outrage came primarily from elements of the right, with conservative commentators and influencers offended that “Brad” was portrayed by a white actor.
Cotton’s unusual exchange with Trumpland wasn’t of his own making. The two-term lawmaker was targeted by Trump in a Truth Social screed that criticized the senator for opposing a bill making daylight saving time permanent. In the post, Trump shared what he said was Cotton’s cellphone number.
Sanders and Cotton aren’t the first Republicans to experience the finicky nature of Trump and other top Republicans.
Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill witnessed that firsthand when Trump abruptly canceled plans to sign bipartisan legislation that Hill crafted as he faced a heated reelection bid. Trump ultimately allowed the bill to become law, but without his signature.
Is there an upside for either Sanders or Cotton? Perhaps. 
Distance from Trump and some elements of the right can’t hurt in an election season where the president’s low approval numbers have put Republican states like Iowa and even South Carolina potentially in play.



Let us know what you think...


 


Cotton and Sanders are still sticking with messages designed to keep their base engaged. Less than a week after the Brad ad, Sanders unveiled two new spots that included one singling out Democratic figures like New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Cotton, meanwhile, has ramped up his attacks on Democratic rival Hallie Shoffner over immigration. 
With Republicans and their allies vastly outspending Democrats in Arkansas, a November upset still feels like a longshot. Aside from a poll showing surprisingly close races for Cotton and Hill, there’s been a dearth of polling in the state. 
A mercurial president and his base, however, add a little more uncertainty.
The danger for Republicans is the Brad ad and daylight saving doxxing are drawing attention to a state that’s mostly stayed off the radar nationally. Meanwhile, national Democrats are investing more in Chris Jones’ bid to unseat Hill and strategist James Carville touting Shoffner’s challenge to Cotton as the midterm’s sleeper race.
The November election is testing how much Arkansas Republicans can withstand a challenging environment for their party nationally. It’s also offering the party a cautionary tale about the limits of being loyal to Trump.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: ICE deported her from CT. Now, she parents from Mexico.
description: Nancy Martinez has filed a lawsuit following her deportation, but even a victory would not allow her to return to her children in the U.S.
text:
Most days, Nancy Martinez hauls a small tent and stacks of carefully folded clothing to a thoroughfare near her home in Naucalpan de Juárez, Mexico. As she’s selling a pair of shoes or a dress, a New Haven number lights up her cellphone. It’s a call from her son’s school. He’s inconsolable again and Martinez’s voice is the only thing that will soothe him.
“It doesn’t matter what I’m doing: I rush to talk to my kids. I’m always there for them,” she said. 
Martinez talks with her 9-year-old son and 14-year-old daughter before school, after school and at bedtime every day. But it’s not enough for the children whose mother used to pack them homemade meals for lunch because they didn’t like the food in the school cafeteria and who insisted on leaving phones and tablets off the table at mealtimes.
It’s not enough for the mother whose hands no longer fold her kids’ clothes but instead stack T-shirts into neat piles to sell to strangers. 
Martinez’s son has autism spectrum disorder. Though he’s usually reserved, lately thoughts about his mom bubble up. “I just want my mom,” he’ll say to a teacher, a stranger, a relative. On a few occasions, he’s walked up to a security guard in the hallway of his school, demanding to know why they took his mother away.
The trauma her children experienced on June 9, 2025 when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents detained her in front of their home — and all they’ve experienced since — motivated Martinez to file a lawsuit against the federal government this summer. She filed with the backing of the Yale Law School Worker and Immigrant Rights Advocacy Clinic.
The family had been headed to school during the last full week of classes before summer break. After she dropped the kids off, Martinez had planned to attend a court appearance. 
But before she could pull away from the curb, three vehicles boxed the family in. As ICE agents yelled at Martinez, who does not speak English, to get out of the car and handcuffed her, her teenage daughter — referred to in court documents as M.A.M. — asked the officers why her mother was being arrested. 
There was a warrant for Martinez’s arrest, the agents told her, though no warrant was shown to the family, according to Martinez’s lawsuit.
“Her children, helpless, witnessed their mother’s abduction,” the complaint says.
Martinez was among roughly 100 people arrested by ICE in Connecticut that June, according to arrest data provided by ICE and published for public use by the Deportation Data Project. She joined the thousands of others who last year were separated from their U.S.-born children as the Trump administration began to fulfill its pledge of mass deportations.
In a Department of Homeland Security statement sent to The Connecticut Mirror, the department said Martinez was in the country illegally and has a criminal history that includes arrests for assault and breach of peace. 
According to Martinez’s lawsuit, the charges stemmed from an argument with her sister-in-law over babysitting. Martinez’s attorneys, Michael Wishnie and Armando Ghinaglia-Socorro, said the state agreed to drop the charges if Martinez attended anger management classes, which she began to do in May 2025. Prosecutors filed to dismiss the case when she was deported, they added.
As Martinez’s son, who is referred to as U.A.M. in court documents, cried on the sidewalk on that June morning, ICE agents pulled Martinez’s hands behind her back. She frantically spoke in Spanish to her daughter as she was handcuffed and put in the back of a black vehicle where, according to the lawsuit, she had her first ever panic attack. 
Martinez’s mother, who was visiting from Mexico at the time, came out of the house when she heard Martinez yelling ‘Mamá!’ She stayed with the children, though the lawsuit alleges that ICE officers never spoke to her or ensured that the children were in appropriate care. 
The lawsuit says it was a breach of duty when ICE forced Martinez into an unmarked vehicle and then “drove off, leaving M.A.M. and U.A.M. standing in the street without a known legal guardian.” The lawsuit says that ICE ignored Martinez’s mother, “refused to tell the children’s father their location” by phone, and “showed little concern for M.A.M. and U.A.M.’s safety and well-being as they took Ms. Martinez away.” 
The DHS statement denied this allegation, calling the claims in the lawsuit “blatantly false.” 
“Before departing the scene, officers confirmed that Martinez’s mother was home and would be able to look after her children,” the statement said.
A month later, Martinez was deported to Mexico. 
Her lawsuit seeks financial damages for the family’s treatment, which it calls “abusive” and “reckless.” But even a victory in that case would not allow Martinez to return to her husband and children in the U.S.

Nora Sandigo speaks to immigrant families with small children Sunday, Jan. 19, 2025, in Miami. Sandigo is the legal guardian to more than 2,000 U.S.-born children of immigrant parents. (AP Photo/Marta Lavandier, file)

Family separations
It’s now been more than a year since Martinez was deported. When she was arrested, her children joined the other 145,000 U.S. children estimated to have been affected by the detention of a parent in the period between January 20, 2025 and April 9, 2026, according to data analyzed by nonpartisan think tank Brookings Institution.
Tara Watson, one of the Brookings researchers, said most of those detained have been deported. When ICE agents took Martinez, it was part of a larger pattern of family separation being replicated across the U.S., Watson said.
“A parent is arrested or detained or deported, and there’s literally no one in any government who is responsible for making sure their child is OK, or even knows who their child is,” Watson said. “The government itself is not collecting this information. They are supposed to ask, and we think it’s only happening sometimes.”
ICE does have a policy — the Detained Parents Directive — that guides agents when they remove parents from children. But the 2025 version of that policy, advocates say, reduces ICE’s responsibilities to keep families together through shifts in language and policy. For example, the previous directive required agents to place detained parents at a facility near their children, whereas under the new directive parents can be moved anywhere.
There’s no single federal agency that’s responsible for the kids that are left behind.Kica Matos, president of the National Immigration Law Center
Kica Matos, president of the National Immigration Law Center, affirmed that while ICE may have guidance for how to care for children when parents are detained, “there’s no single federal agency that’s responsible for the kids that are left behind,” she said. “In practice, no one is clearly accountable.” 
The state’s Department of Children and Families does not typically have a role in these cases because parents and children are not being separated due to abuse or neglect.
Matos is among those encouraging families to proactively plan, including by completing Connecticut’s standby guardian designation form, to ensure that children go to the caretaker of a parent’s choosing in such a situation. Connecticut has created a webpage to give families more information on the process, and some immigrant advocacy organizations are also holding trainings to guide families on what documents they might need if parents are separated from their children.  When a family chooses to transfer guardianship because a parent has been deported, that arrangement can also be formalized through probate court proceedings. 

A U.S.-born toddler sits on her mother’s lap as Nora Sandigo, who runs a non-profit dedicated to supporting immigrant families, explains migrants’ legal rights and options to prepare their families in case a parent were to be detained or deported, Friday, Jan. 17, 2025, in Homestead, Fla. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)

In March, U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., co-authored a report, “Cruelty is the Point: How Trump’s Immigration Agenda Endangers Children,” which reviewed 128 cases of children “who have been injured, left unattended, or otherwise put at direct risk of harm as a result” of DHS actions. The report includes an instance of a 1-year-old girl left alone in her car seat by ICE agents who detained the child’s father, and another instance of children watching their father get detained as he was taking them to school. 
Blumenthal said Martinez’s case in particular has struck a nerve because of “the absolute cruelty of seizing her while taking her children to school without any notice or warning,” he said. “But also then listening to her, as we did at the press conference, and hearing her heartbreak, as well as her confusion and her loneliness. I mean, just absolutely crushing sadness that I felt during her talk about how much she misses her children and her family.”
In its statement after Martinez’s arrest, federal officials said ICE “does not separate families. 
“Parents are asked if they want to be removed with their children or ICE will place the children with a safe person the parent designates,” the statement said. “This is consistent with past administration’s immigration enforcement.” 
But Martinez told the CT Mirror that she was not asked if she wanted to be removed with her children when she was detained or during her time in a detention center.
DHS also said the U.S. offers money — $2,600 — and a free flight to people who came into the country illegally to self-deport. “We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return,” the statement said.
At a press conference about ICE activity on Oct. 1 in New Haven, Glenn Formica, a Connecticut attorney with the American Immigrant Legal Clinic, said that in his experience, DHS isn’t making good on that promise. 
“They will promise them money, and then the money for leaving never shows,” he said. “It’s just deceit.” 
DHS did not respond to CT Mirror’s recent questions about its policies.
In a September letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy , D-Conn., pressed for information about whether ICE agents were in fact following the Detained Parents Directive during each arrest. 
“If so, what evidence can you provide that arresting agents/officers followed such policy? If not, provide a written rationale for such deviation,” he wrote. 
Murphy has also authored bills that would prohibit ICE from conducting operations at locations where children are present, like school bus stops and day care centers. 
Martinez’s case has remained top of mind for advocates like Matos.
“The way that Nancy was detained was a real crystallization and an affirmation of the brutality of this administration’s deportation agenda,” Matos said. “Never before had we seen what we saw that day — which is what we had heard was happening around the country — manifested in New Haven. ICE blocking people in their cars, wearing masks in people’s neighborhoods, handcuffing people and taking them away in the most frightening way possible.” 

Nancy Martinez poses for a portrait at her family home in Naucalpan, State of Mexico, Mexico. Tuesday, July 8, 2025.

Shattered dreams
After she was arrested, Martinez spent about a month in detention at the Wyatt Detention Facility in Rhode Island before she was deported to the border city of Matamoros. From there, she got on a flight to Mexico City, and returned to her family home in nearby Naucalpan de Juárez, in a neighborhood called El Universal. 
“When I came back to Mexico, all of my dreams were shattered,” she said. Upon returning to her native country, “I didn‘t think about the sounds or the smells, I spent my time weeping,” she said. 
She returned to a family home and was reunited with her two oldest children for the first time in more than a decade.
Martinez had cared for her oldest kids as a single mom in Mexico. But she reunited with her first love in her early 20s and the couple decided to move to the U.S., in hopes of building a better life. “I couldn’t provide for my children’s needsin Mexico’s economy,” Martinez said of her decision.
But she said the trip into the U.S. would have been dangerous for her oldest children, who were 3 and 5 at the time. “I didn’t want to cross the border with them because of how many things can go horribly wrong on that journey,” she said.
She said she also had no one to care for them in the U.S. while she and her partner worked so she “entrusted them to the care of my mother and grandmother so that I could go provide for them.”
Martinez sent money back to her family in Mexico for the children’s needs and so they could attend private school. 
In Connecticut, Martinez had her two youngest children. But even as she missed the children she left with family in Mexico, she was intent on making her sacrifice meaningful. 
“I don’t regret it. I’ve been asked if I would do it again — and yes I would. It was a better life,” she said. 
After her deportation, the National Immigration Law Center helped fundraise to buy tickets for U.A.M. and M.A.M. to fly to Mexico and spend this past summer with Martinez. During their visit, four generations of the family were together under one roof. 
Martinez’s family home, constructed on land her grandmother purchased, is large enough to house extended family. Martinez has her own area of the house on the second floor where she keeps her inventory of clothes to sell. Downstairs, Martinez’s mother has a small shop where she sells soda, snacks and basic household supplies. 
“This is a humble neighborhood,” Martinez said. “There’s a lot of poverty — too much.” Around 40% of the Naucalpan de Juárez’s residents live in poverty, which Martinez sees plainly from the door of her home. People struggling with substance use live under tents within view of a ravine that’s sometimes used as a dump site for trash. 
The home is full of framed family photographs and Catholic iconography: an image of the Virgen de Guadalupe looks out on the hallway in front of Martinez’s bedroom and a shrine with a crucifix and angelic dolls dressed in white satin is tucked into another nook. In a spare room where Martinez stores her inventory of clothing and accessories, framed portraits show the family at key moments over decades: weddings and quinceañeras, the 15th birthday celebration for girls from many Latin American countries that’s celebrated with an elaborate party and a colorful ballgown with a voluminous skirt. 
Martinez herself never wanted a quinceañera. But her daughters — one in Mexico and one in the U.S. — did. Now, years after missing her eldest daughter’s quinceañeñera in Mexico, she will miss her younger daughter’s celebration in Connecticut when M.A.M. turns 15 in January. 
Since her mother was deported, M.A.M. has struggled to focus on her schoolwork and has taken on significant responsibilities to help raise U.A.M, according to Martinez’s lawsuit. “Shouldering the weight of being a growing teenager and now a caregiver has taken its toll,” the lawsuit states. “Following her mother’s abduction, M.A.M. became a shell of herself, uncharacteristically irritable, reticent and withdrawn.” 
M.A.M.’s has long dreamed of a quinceañera party, but after her mother’s deportation, it was hard to imagine celebrating anything. The details were overwhelming too: there was the question of the cost, and the logistics of planning a party on the scale of a wedding — with music, food, choreographed dances and the magnificent dress — without Martinez there to help. When they first discussed it, Martinez’s husband said it wouldn’t work. But after the shock of deportation wore off, her conviction grew: “I told him, ‘no — we can’t take this dream away from her.’” 
When the children visited Mexico this summer, Martinez and M.A.M. worked on planning the party. Even as she organizes the details, it’s precisely the type of milestone that hurts most for Martinez to miss. 
We need our mom. I’m only 13 — I’m not going to be able to handle this all alone.Nancy martinez’s teenage daughter
At least some of those moments have come unexpectedly in the year since Martinez was detained. Just days after Martinez’s arrest, M.A.M. stood before a crowd in downtown New Haven and spoke through tears about her mother. 
“We need our mom. I’m only 13 — I’m not going to be able to handle this all alone,” she said, speaking quickly. “You’re not just doing this to my family, you’re hurting other immigrant families who need their parents back home. You’re causing a lot of pain to these families by taking them away.” Her face crumpled with tears as Matos embraced her. 
From inside a detention center, Martinez heard a TV broadcasting her daughter’s voice. “That’s my daughter, she’s the one who’s talking!” Martinez remembered saying. “Oh wow, she expresses herself so well.” 
It’s one of the qualities in M.A.M. that Martinez has always been proud of.
When the lawsuit was announced in June of this year, M.A.M. and U.A.M. sat in a room at Yale Law School for another press conference. On a screen at the front of the room, Martinez spoke through an interpreter, telling the story of how ICE took her a year earlier, explaining the cognitive dissonance of that day. 
“As a mother, I take pride in being a planner, coordinating my work schedule around teacher conferences, doctor’s appointments and sports matches, but nothing, absolutely nothing could have prepared me for what I saw looking out the window: there were my children clinging to their grandma and crying out for me as I got farther and farther away,” she said.
Since that moment, Martinez said, she has longed to hold her children through moments of “heartbreak, confusion and loneliness.” 
Then, it was M.A.M.’s turn to speak. She walked calmly to the podium and read from prepared comments, rushing through as if trying to outrun the emotion of the moment.  
“No one should have to go through what my family and I have gone through the past year,” she said quietly. “When ICE took away my mom, they took away my best friend. My confident and hardworking parent. My provider and my safety.” 
M.A.M. has taken on responsibilities beyond her years, the lawsuit says. It details how in the summers, she now sells flan and chocolate-covered strawberries to help support the family. She also soothes her brother when he wakes up from nightmares, no longer able to sleep in his own bedroom “out of fear that someone will also take his sister away.”  
U.A.M. sat in the audience and watched his big sister speak. She told the attorneys and TV cameras of her worries for him. 
“He is still young, and everything has been so rough on him,” she said. “He is constantly scared, and now never wants to leave my side.”
Thousands of miles away, Martinez watched the press conference until the livestream shut off.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PAID POST: How Connecticut Hospitals Are Modernizing Critical Infrastructure for the Future
description: Connecticut healthcare systems are modernizing critical energy infrastructure to improve reliability, increase efficiency, and support patient care for years to come.
text:
When people visit a hospital, their attention is understandably focused on the care they receive. They see doctors, nurses, specialists, and support staff working together to improve lives. What most patients don’t usually see is the extensive infrastructure operating behind the scenes that makes the care they are receiving possible.
Power generation systems, heating and cooling equipment, utility plants, and other critical facilities support every aspect of hospital operations. Much of this infrastructure operates around the clock and requires ongoing investment to remain reliable, efficient, and resilient.
For healthcare organizations across Connecticut, maintaining and modernizing these systems presents a growing challenge. As facilities age and technology advances, healthcare providers must make significant infrastructure investments while continuing to direct resources toward their primary mission: caring for patients.
CT Children’s Medical Center, a CHEFA financing supported the construction of a new tower that  includes two floors with 50 private neonatal intensive care rooms, a fetal care center with six labor, delivery, recovery and postpartum rooms, as well as two dedicated operating rooms, and an advanced gene therapy unit where bone marrow transplants and liquid radiation treatments can be performed.  Credit: CHEFA
Increasingly, healthcare systems are exploring new approaches that allow them to address both priorities at once.
One example is Hartford HealthCare’s recently announced energy modernization initiative, which is being financed through an innovative Energy-as-a-Service model facilitated by the Connecticut Health and Educational Facilities Authority (CHEFA). Through a 30-year partnership with ENFRA Solutions, Hartford HealthCare is undertaking a comprehensive effort to modernize key energy infrastructure across its healthcare network, including renewal of the co-generation facility at Hartford Hospital.
The initiative is expected to generate more than $11 million in annual utility savings while enhancing the reliability and efficiency of systems that support critical healthcare operations every day.
The project also reflects a broader shift in how some institutions are approaching infrastructure management. By partnering with specialized operators to oversee complex energy systems, healthcare organizations can reduce operational burdens and focus more attention and resources on delivering care, improving patient experiences, and meeting evolving community needs.
LiveWell, CHEFA financing supported transformative dementia care improvements, including the addition of private nursing beds to a new Center for Resilient Living. Credit: CHEFA
For Connecticut residents, investments like these may be largely invisible, but their impact is tangible. Reliable energy infrastructure helps hospitals remain operational during emergencies, supports long-term sustainability goals, and creates efficiencies that can strengthen an organization’s ability to serve patients well into the future.
As healthcare systems continue to navigate changing demands, innovative financing solutions are providing new pathways for modernization. By helping nonprofit organizations access capital for strategic infrastructure investments, CHEFA supports projects that strengthen essential community institutions while helping them remain focused on the people they serve.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas may surprise the nation and elect a Democrat to the US Senate. MAGA politics reshaped state.
description: In 1932, Kansas voters elected Democrat George McGill to the U.S Senate. In the 32 senate elections since then, voters have consistently elected Republicans to represent them. This historic streak makes Democrat Adam Hamilton’s bid to prevail in his challenge to the reelection of U.S. Senator Roger Marshall an uphill climb. However, Marshall’s embrace of […]
text:
Adam Hamilton answers questions at a Kansas Chamber forum on Aug. 27, 2026, in Olathe. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)In 1932, Kansas voters elected Democrat George McGill to the U.S Senate. In the 32 senate elections since then, voters have consistently elected Republicans to represent them.
This historic streak makes Democrat Adam Hamilton’s bid to prevail in his challenge to the reelection of U.S. Senator Roger Marshall an uphill climb. However, Marshall’s embrace of MAGA politics has changed the dynamics of the race and given Hamilton a credible shot at a dramatic upset.
History shows that the leading GOP senators Kansas voters sent to Washington have been genuine legislators — pragmatic, problem-solving, middle-of-the-road Republicans who have chosen bipartisan solutions for public issues.
Adam Hamilton says “we need to stop the chaos and corruption in Washington by actually listening to people and working together to get things done for Kansas families.”
He vows to “lead from the middle” and avoid extreme positions on the right or the left.
His philosophy closely aligns with Kansas’ Republican senators over past years.
Let’s take a closer look.
Kansas voters have elected and reelected 11 individuals as Republican senators since 1932. The first four of those had served as governor of Kansas before their election to the U.S. Senate. Three of the four (Arthur Capper, Clyde Reed and Frank Carlson) had roots in progressive-era politics. They were activists and problem solvers who understood the give and take of the legislative process — experience that served them well in the U.S. Senate.
Kansas Senator Jim Pearson, first elected in 1962, was characterized by a dedicated staff member as a “man in the middle” who worked effectively with leading Senate Democrats.
Pearson and Democrat Walter Mondale initiated reform of the filibuster rule in the U.S. Senate, which eventually led in 1983 to lowering the threshold to close debate in the chamber from a two-thirds to a three-fifths vote.
As ranking member of the aviation subcommittee of the Senate Commerce Committee, Pearson joined forces with committee Democrats to establish an airport-airways trust fund, similar to the highway trust fund, to provide for modernization of the nation’s airports and airways, while also protecting the aviation industry in Kansas.
Bob Dole evolved over his five elections to the U.S. Senate, 1968 through 1992, from a fierce partisan and Nixon ally into a formidable bipartisan force to address critical issues and get things done.
In 1977, for example, Dole and Democrat George McGovern, respectively ranking member and chair of the Senate Agriculture Committee, worked hand in hand to build bipartisan support and substantially reform and expand the food stamp program.
Most importantly, in the early 1980s, Dole worked with Democrat Patrick Moynihan to break a legislative gridlock that eventually led to major reforms and secured future funding of Social Security.
Nancy Landon Kassebaum, first elected in 1978, partnered with Democrat Ted Kennedy in securing enactment of legislation that helped to assure that employees losing their jobs would not lose health insurance.
Kassebaum also championed the protection of public lands through the establishment of the Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve in the Flint Hills of Kansas.
Kansas Senator Roger Marshall stands in stark contrast to these Kansas senators. During his 10 years in congress, he has gravitated toward unyielding partisanship and become a proponent of MAGA’s culture wars.
Marshall lent critical support to Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill, which the Congressional Budget Office estimates will slash more than $1 trillion in spending from Medicaid and food assistance for the next 10 years, primarily by restricting eligibility for aid. Ten to 12 million people will be cut from Medicaid, and those qualified for food assistance will drop as well.
Marshall gave his approval to Trump nominees who were unqualified for their positions, such as Robert Kennedy Jr, Kristi Noem and Pete Hegseth, among others.
He has given unqualified support to Trump’s war on Iran, which has raised pump prices to $4 and diesel to $6. He has repeatedly voted to block congressional measures to end the war.
Marshall has stated that Trump’s chaotic on-again-off-again tariffs are working, when in fact those actions are elevating inflation at the grocery store for everyday Kansans. He appears to represent the Trump administration rather than Kansans in the U.S. Senate. He avoids public forums with Kansans, which he claims to be “dangerous.”
His partisan conduct has given Kansas voters a clear choice in the U.S. Senate race.
Voters may just choose to break from the streak of the past 32 senate elections and surprise the nation.
H. Edward Flentje is a professor emeritus at Wichita State University and formerly was director and professor in the Hugo Wall School of Public Affairs at the university. He has written and edited numerous publications, including most recently co-writing and co-editing “Reform and Reaction: The Arc of Kansas Politics.” Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The final boarding call
description: Let’s take a moment of silence to remember the airlines that are no more.
text:
Planning a flight soon? With fewer airlines to choose among (including newcomers Avelo and Breeze, both with bases in Connecticut), let’s take a moment of silence to remember the carriers that are no more.
Seatbacks and tray tables in their upright positions, please. It’s going to be a bumpy ride.



Do you remember PEOPLExpress Airlines? How about NorthEast? Or Mohawk? These airlines of the past are what we call “fallen flags,” remembered, perhaps, but no longer in business, at least not under those names. The U.S. domestic airline industry is littered with such unclaimed baggage of our traveling past and each one brings back memories of a time when flying was fun and a middle seat came with a meal, not just a fee.
Newark-based PEOPLExpress was a favorite of mine, flying out of the ancient North Terminal and charging super-low fares which were collected in-flight. Like many carriers they grew too big, too fast and were snapped up by aviation pariah Frank Lorenzo.
We also had Pan Am, Eastern, TWA, Northwest and Continental, each gobbled up or merged with much larger carriers leaving us with, some say, a much less competitive (and more expensive) travel industry.
Recent airline closures include ultra-low-cost carrier Spirit, the airline that taught us to pay for checked bags. Hawaiian still flies, but under its acquirer Alaska Airlines’ code. Some of the lost carriers were airlines within an airline, like Song (Delta’s low cost carrier, targeted specifically at women) or Ted (a no-frills subset of United).
Texas-based Braniff had the distinction of being the only U.S. airline to fly the Concorde (albeit on a lease from Air France and British Airways and flown subsonic over U.S. airspace). Braniff’s jets were painted in bold colors by Alexander Calder, their flight attendants uniforms designed by Emilio Pucci.
A slew of regional carriers long ago made their final boarding calls: Mohawk (taken over by Allegheny, itself subsumed into USAir which in turn was bought by American). Piedmont was also grabbed by USAir. North Central and Southern Airlines became Republic, which bought Hughes Airwest before getting picked up by Northwest, formerly known as Northwest Orient.
Air Florida flew for 13 years, even flying to seven European cities. And you might remember ValuJet which merged with AirTran. Tower Air made a name for itself (and good money) flying charters for the Pentagon while also providing cheap transcontinental service from JFK to the West Coast. Four other carriers, World Airways, Capitol, ONA (Overseas National) and Trans International, also became successful charter lines for civilians and the military.
Carnival Airlines, owned by the cruise ship line, funneled passengers to its own ships on charters and was later acquired by a reorganized Pan Am.
Midwest was a favorite for many, offering fresh baked cookies inflight in comfy two-by-two seating on their DC-9s. But there were also regional carriers Vanguard, Air South, Eastwind and McClain airlines.
For crossing the “pond” there were a number of failed airlines that offered business-class comfort at bargain fares: Eos, MaxJet and SilverJet. Still flying is one of my favorites, French airline La Compagnie which flies just 76 passengers on an A-321neo that can usually carry over 200, at less than traditional business-class fares.
Domestically MGM Grand Air was popular with the Hollywood crowd, flying from LAX to JFK in a lavishly equipped DC-8 with couches and such.
When smoking was banned on U.S. flights starting in 1988, the Tobacco Institute talked about starting a smokers-only airline, but that never happened.
One airline that did fly, for a couple of years, was Hooters Air, owned by the restaurant chain. In-flight cabin staff on the golfer-targeted flights to Myrtle Beach wore the same skimpy attire as the restaurant’s waitresses. Hardly PC, never profitable and, thankfully, short-lived.
Yes… flying used to be fun and cheap. But now it’s neither.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Trump touts Memphis law enforcement surge in Tennessee rally meant to shore up midterm support
description: CLARKSVILLE, Tenn. — The rainy remnants of Hurricane Isaias didn’t deter Tennessee Republicans from turning out Saturday to hear President Donald Trump decry state Democrats as “communists” and “socialists,” and praise Tennessee’s federal delegation and the success of the Memphis Safe Task Force.  “I got a call from your governor, I got a call from […]
text:
President Donald Trump made his second visit to Tennessee in as many weeks, stopping in Clarksville on Oct. 10, 2026, to urge Republicans to vote in the upcoming midterm election. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)CLARKSVILLE, Tenn. — The rainy remnants of Hurricane Isaias didn’t deter Tennessee Republicans from turning out Saturday to hear President Donald Trump decry state Democrats as “communists” and “socialists,” and praise Tennessee’s federal delegation and the success of the Memphis Safe Task Force. 
“I got a call from your governor, I got a call from the mayor of Memphis, they said ‘We need your help, it’s out of control,’” Trump said.
The president referred to the coalition of federal and state agencies deployed in September 2025 to Memphis, Tennessee’s second-largest city. 
Trump made his second visit in as many weeks to the Volunteer State, speaking to a crowd of about 4,500 inside Clarksville’s 6,000-seat FM Bank Arena. He took the stage 45 minutes past the scheduled 2:30 p.m. start time to the tune of “Proud to Be An American,” the 1984 Lee Greenwood song that has become an anthem of sorts for Republicans. 
Political experts predict Trump’s sagging poll ratings and economic angst spurred by the war in Iran and rising grocery and gas prices could lead to Democrats taking the U.S. House back after waging competitive campaigns in traditionally red states, including Texas, for the Senate. Yet, the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan news outlet analyzing state and federal elections, rates all of Tennessee’s congressional seats as ‘Solidly Republican.’
During a 95-minute speech, Trump ranged back and forth between topics but hewed to themes familiar to followers, including crime, immigration enforcement and claims of rigged elections. 
An April analysis from ProPublica and MLK50, a Memphis outlet, found only 2% of immigration arrests in Memphis were for violent crime, even as detention of immigrants has surged there and across the state since Trump took office in January 2024. 
Agents with the Memphis law enforcement force have shot and killed four men since May. It includes the Tennessee Highway Patrol, Tennessee National Guard, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the U.S. Marshals Service.
Trump’s visit to Tennessee came as part of a monthlong blitz to shore up the GOP’s chances in the midterms. In Clarksville, he praised U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican nominee for governor, U.S. Sen. Bill Hagerty, who is up for reelection and members of the congressional delegation, urging attendees to vote. 
“The communists, socialists, Democrats, they will cheat, they will do whatever,” Trump said. 
Blackburn and Hagerty joined Trump on stage, as did all of Tennessee’s GOP congressmen with the exception of 5th Congressional District U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles, who lost in the August primary to former state Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher. 
Blackburn, the last of a roster of Republican elected officials to speak before the president entered, called her Democratic opponent Jerri Green a “radical socialist” and characterized independent gubernatorial candidates David Hatley and Lauren Pinkston as Democrats. 

“I’m the only conservative Republican in the race,” she said. 
Speakers included U.S. Reps. Matt Van Epps of the 7th Congressional District and Scott DesJarlais of the 4th, state Sen. Brent Taylor, running for the 9th Congressional District, state Rep. Johnny Garrett, the Republican nominee in the 4th Congressional District and state House Speaker Cameron Sexton. 
A Reuters/Ipsos poll released this week found Trump’s approval ratings at record lows. 
Outside the arena, a clutch of protesters yelled at Trump-backers to “stay on your side of the street,” a man hawked red “Make America Great Again” hats and Blackburn campaign volunteers handed out yard signs. 
Jenna Baggett, 20, of Dickson and a student at University of South Alabama, which Trump visited on Oct. 2, scrunched her face when asked if she was excited to vote for Blackburn. 

“I’m not excited,” Baggett said. “But I’ll vote for her.”
