name: Oklahoma Voice
title: A rural Oklahoma hospital is bringing back maternity care. Can it survive healthcare cuts?
description: On the last day of August, Julie Schroeder was one day away from giving birth to a baby girl. The 25-year-old Arnett resident didn’t know it, because she wanted to go into labor naturally and deliver with the provider she saw during pregnancy. But that meant planning for a nearly two-hour drive southeast to Weatherford […]
text:
Newman Memorial's CEO Tom Vasko and Amy Calhoun-Vasko stand in Newman Memorial Hospital's future labor-and-delivery unit on Aug. 31. (Photo by Jillian Taylor/StateImpact Oklahoma)On the last day of August, Julie Schroeder was one day away from giving birth to a baby girl. The 25-year-old Arnett resident didn’t know it, because she wanted to go into labor naturally and deliver with the provider she saw during pregnancy. But that meant planning for a nearly two-hour drive southeast to Weatherford Regional Hospital.


Schroeder had seen Amy Calhoun-Vasko at Newman Memorial Hospital up until 26 weeks. The certified nurse midwife is about 20 minutes away in Shattuck. After that timeframe, Calhoun-Vasko can continue seeing her patients at Weatherford Regional, where she delivers babies. It’s one way she has adapted to Newman Memorial not having labor and delivery.
The hospital’s last delivery was in 2015. Several physicians retired around that time, and when only one remained, it was “too much to handle,” Calhoun-Vasko said.
Today, only 27% of Oklahoma’s rural hospitals offer labor and delivery services amid workforce shortages and financial pressures. In 2024, about half of Oklahoma’s counties had zero obstetric clinicians. And according to the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform, payments from private insurance plans and Medicaid programs often don’t cover the cost of delivering safe, high-quality maternity care.
About four years ago, Calhoun-Vasko and her husband, Tom Vasko, left Virginia to work in rural Oklahoma. In a job interview before Vasko became Newman Memorial’s CEO, he was told the critical access hospital wanted its next leader to meet a seemingly insurmountable goal: bring labor and delivery back.
Since then, the couple has worked to obtain a few million dollars to get started. Vasko said the door has been slammed in their faces many times. But that is about to change.
The Northwest Oklahoma hospital plans to restore this service next year, using money from a five-year, $50 billion federal investment meant to transform rural healthcare across the U.S.
Newman Memorial hopes the model it’s building can sustain access despite nearly $1 trillion in looming reductions to federal Medicaid spending over a decade, signed into law last year alongside the dollars fueling its project.
Restoring maternity care

	Oklahoma received more than $223 million from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for its first year of funding under the Rural Health Transformation Program. The state’s plan features 29 initiatives, including the Rural Regional Reorientation Program, under which Newman Memorial is receiving $1.4 million, Vasko said.
It’s intended to improve access to local and specialty care, and reduce disease and avoidable hospitalizations.
Vasko said the dollars will go toward infrastructure like beds, monitors, equipment and surgical needs. Because it’s reimbursement-based, the critical access hospital has applied for additional opportunities to secure upfront funding. The goal is to have infrastructure in place by January and launch sometime next year, Vasko said.
“If you’d asked me three and a half years ago, I wanted to walk in the door and deliver a baby the next day,” Calhoun-Vasko said. “Three and a half years later, I now realize that we were not ready for that, and we needed this time period to build up to that.”
The hospital has implemented lactation and mental health services for maternity care and hired a doula.
Once Newman Memorial opens its labor-and-delivery unit, Calhoun-Vasko will handle low-risk births. She said about 85% of pregnant patients fall into the category appropriate for her care. A group of OB-GYNs will rotate weekly and cover high-risk deliveries and gynecological surgeries, bringing a needed service to Northwest Oklahoma and revenue to Newman.
Dr. Zach Wohlgemuth hopes to be one of those OB-GYNs. He is a medical director at a hospital in North Carolina and Calhoun-Vasko’s former coworker. His facility has implemented a similar midwifery-forward model, including several midwives and physicians. He said this structure helps clinicians work at their maximum capacity to serve patients.
Wohlgemuth said he appreciates that the physician team Newman Memorial is assembling won’t rely on a staffing company. Instead, several consistent, core doctors will work alongside Calhoun-Vasko in the town of 1,212 people.
“People care who deliver their babies, and they want continuity in that care. And that’s important to them,” Wohlgemuth said. “Especially in small towns.”
Newman Memorial is set to become Oklahoma’s second critical access hospital to deliver babies. Darin Farrell, CEO of Weatherford Regional Hospital, said his critical access facility isn’t the first to offer the service, but it is the only one remaining.
Medicare pays critical access hospitals based on cost. Because of that, Farrell said it can be financially counterproductive for them to deliver babies. In 2025, Medicaid covered around half of Oklahoma births, and about 42% were paid for by private insurance, according to data from the State Department of Health.
But Farrell said the service has always been a priority in Weatherford.
“Even in very, very lean times, financially speaking, the hospital leadership and the medical community, the physicians, have seen it as a vital component of what we do at the hospital,” Farrell said.
The hospital has benefited from a steady group of physicians to help maintain labor and delivery. Farrell said its partnership with certified nurse midwife Calhoun-Vasko is a first. But he’s seen how the setup can be beneficial.
A Weatherford patient went into labor during Calhoun-Vasko’s first weekend covering labor and delivery. While she handled the delivery, the patient’s physician got to continue coaching his child’s soccer game.
The physician told Farrell the patient might have been one he would have taken into C-section earlier than Calhoun-Vasko would have. The patient ended up delivering vaginally.
“That model is something that now we will continue to do in the future and be much more open to it than we had been in the past,” Farrell said.
Growing midwifery care

	Farrell, a registered nurse, said he didn’t have experience working with certified nurse midwives before Calhoun-Vasko. The providers hold graduate degrees and are advanced-practice registered nurses who specialize in primary, sexual and reproductive care.
“I’ve come to realize that even if nurses have a nursing background or physicians have gone and received their education, they still have a lack of knowledge in regards to certified nurse midwives,” said Priscilla McFolling, the program director of The Midwifery Project.
The Oklahoma Perinatal Quality Improvement Collaborative program works to expand the state’s midwifery capacity. According to the March of Dimes, midwifery care can reduce interventions and health care costs, and increase patient satisfaction.
Oklahoma had 86 certified nurse midwives as of August, and McFolling said they aren’t being used to their full potential.
Only 12 of Oklahoma’s 41 birthing hospitals have integrated the providers, she said. A report from the State Department of Health notes that midwifery care is well established in tribal facilities, and it can be a viable option for low-risk pregnancies in areas with provider shortages.
“I feel like midwives are definitely a part of that solution for how we can ensure that our women of reproductive age, pregnant women, can have that high-quality care from a provider,” McFolling said.
Barbara O’Brien, director of the Oklahoma Perinatal Quality Improvement Collaborative, said she hopes Newman Memorial’s model will succeed and can be replicated in other hospitals.
“For example, can McCurtain County start providing obstetrical services again? Could one of the hospitals out in the Panhandle provide obstetric services again, so that their people don’t have to drive all over?” O’Brien said. “Or could they bring midwives out there at least that have prenatal care that they can provide? So [there are] different options that might be available in the future for the different communities in rural Oklahoma.”
Cuts to Medicaid

	As Newman Memorial prepares to launch maternity care, CEO Tom Vasko said it will also be fighting against federal Medicaid cuts, which will impact Oklahoma’s directed payment program. It helps bring hospital reimbursements for serving certain Medicaid patients closer to private insurance rates.
Oklahoma Hospital Association President and CEO Rich Rasmussen said in an email the cuts are designed to begin hitting states on Jan. 1, 2028. Because Oklahoma’s directed payment program was reduced this year, he said the actual cuts will now begin Jan. 1, 2029.
Payments will be phased down by 10% every year until they reach 100% of the Medicare rate.
“That’s what really enables critical access hospitals to keep OB care going and alive is to offset that loss of being underpaid by Medicaid to kind of true up to at least get us to break even. And that’s what DPP does,” Vasko said. “I think it’s also very important that, as we have a change of command and governorship this coming year, that both our candidates really give that some thought.”
Farrell said the Rural Health Transformation Program is a great opportunity for hospitals like Newman Memorial to bring back labor and delivery services that they stopped providing years ago. But to sustain access, he said providers need better Medicaid payments.
“It eventually becomes a decision of, ‘Do we keep the hospital open? Do we continue to provide an emergency room for the community?’ And, for many of the hospitals over the years that close their OB services, that’s the decision it came down to is, ‘We can’t afford to do OB anymore,'” Farrell said.
Despite all of the challenges Vasko and Calhoun-Vasko faced to get to this point, they said nothing has made them want to give up. They’re sustained by passion and stories like that of Jean Foreman and her daughter, Nancy Brookshire. This year, Brookshire celebrated her 70th birthday with Foreman at Newman Memorial, where her mom welcomed her into the world.
“It shows just how the hospital impacts a family across multiple generations – from birth through the entire lifespan,” Vasko said.
Now that they have funding behind them, Vasko said he has no doubt they’ll accomplish their goal, and newborn cries will echo through their halls once again.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: A survived execution in Tennessee exposes the grim science of lethal injection
description: It took Christa Pike nearly a week to regain consciousness after the Tennessee Department of Corrections failed to kill her with two doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital, a drug used to put animals to death and to execute humans by lethal injection in Tennessee and other states. She was confused and angry. She couldn’t eat […]
text:
Randy Spivey and Luke Ihnen, lawyers for Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike, update a gaggle of local and national media on her condition after a Sept. 30 botched execution. (Photo: John/Partipilo) It took Christa Pike nearly a week to regain consciousness after the Tennessee Department of Corrections failed to kill her with two doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital, a drug used to put animals to death and to execute humans by lethal injection in Tennessee and other states.
She was confused and angry. She couldn’t eat because of damage to her throat, she couldn’t move her arms, and her hands were swollen to where they looked like “surgical gloves,” according to one of her attorneys. It was noted during and immediately after the execution attempt that skin on her arms was chemically burned by the high alkalinity of the drug. 
But by Oct. 8, she was “walking with assistance,” according to a memo circulated by her attorneys to federal defenders around the country on Thursday, “and her arms — which sustained significant injuries during the execution attempt — are healing and regaining movement and strength. Her lungs are clear, and she has started to eat a regular diet. Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery.”
Pike’s attorneys and medical advisors had warned that Pike had a blood disorder, and that it had always been difficult for medical staff to draw blood from her veins, let alone insert IV lines. During the execution, after several failed attempts, the technicians placed a needle that most likely collapsed the vein. The bulk of the killing drugs likely went into the tissue around the needles placed in her arms.
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike receiving medical care after failed execution

“I think Christa didn’t die because most of the pentobarbital didn’t get into her brain,” said Dr. Joel Zivot, an Emory University anesthesiology professor who consulted with Pike’s legal team. “It ended up in her arms, so she never had a high enough blood level to kill her. That was the reason — not that she has some capacity to resist pentobarbital. It’s because it just never got into her brain.”
At least not enough to kill her.
The email to federal defenders cautioned that Pike “continues to experience cognitive challenges with concentration and memory. Her physicians have cautioned that it may take months to fully understand whether she sustained lasting cognitive injuries.”
And the burning on her arms belies another frequent problem with pentobarbital used in executions: It is highly caustic. When the drug does flow properly through the veins, the dying prisoner may appear to be sleeping, but in the majority of cases, studies have found that the pentobarbital solution is disintegrating the prisoners’ lungs, burning them apart, causing the condemned prisoners to literally drown in their own body fluids. 
That all happens before the drug has a chance to kill the way it is intended to.
“It’s supposed to stop your breathing,” Zivot said. “But it’s supposed to stop it in your brain. This is different. I think the caustic nature of the solution is separate from what’s killing you. The pentobarbital works on the brain and the heart, and that’s killing you. But it’s what it’s cut with that I think is burning your lungs.”
The syndrome is called flash pulmonary edema, and it theoretically produces a sensation similar to waterboarding. In a deposition in federal court in 2019, Gail Van Norman, a researcher at the University of Washington, called it “one of the most powerful, excruciating feelings known to man.” Van Norman studied 27 autopsies of executed prisoners and found evidence of pulmonary edema in 20 of them.
Some researchers posit that the dying prisoners may still be able to feel the pain, even if they are too sedated to react. Of course, no one has lived to confirm that theory. And there is no news yet whether Pike experienced it.
Zivot’s own research found pulmonary edema in 33 of 43 executions carried out with pentobarbital or midazolam. The identifying symptoms in autopsies are lungs that are up to three times normal weight and the presence of a pink, frothy liquid in the respiratory tree. The froth, Zivot said, is an indication that the person is still struggling to breathe at the point of onset.
What is pentobarbital?
Pentobarbital is used in clinical settings to treat epileptic seizures and also as an anesthesia. It is made by a European pharmaceutical company and marketed under the brand name Nembutal. But the manufacturer will not sell it for use in executions, so corrections departments buy it on the gray market as pentobarbital salts, which then have to be converted into an injectable liquid form by a compounding pharmacy.
In January 2025, during the final days of the Biden administration, the U.S. Department of Justice issued a warning about pentobarbital in executions, citing multiple studies about pulmonary edema. Outgoing Attorney General Merrick Garland had ordered its use stopped.
But in April 2026, the Trump DOJ countered those warnings. After a long preamble about misguided Biden policies, it declared them “wrong on the standard” and “wrong on the science,” and quoted its own expert who said the pulmonary edema didn’t matter because the prisoners were already brain dead, a claim that has not been scientifically settled.
When lethal injection was first used to replace the electric chair and the gas chamber in the 1970s, it used a three-drug process: the anesthetic sodium thiopental to render the prisoner unconscious, followed by a paralytic drug to ensure the prisoner didn’t breathe or show any signs of discomfort, and a final killing dose of potassium chloride that stopped the heart.
But by 2010, thiopental was no longer manufactured in the U.S. and could not be imported. It had been largely replaced in clinical settings by newer drugs. 
Then the pharmaceutical companies balked at selling pentobarbital for use in executions, and corrections departments had to look elsewhere. 
After botched execution of Christa Pike, Tennessee correction chief steps down

A long road back
When Katie Hobbs took the Arizona governor’s office in 2023, she engaged David Duncan, a retired federal magistrate judge, to conduct a study of execution procedures, which had been problematic under long-time prisons director Charles Ryan and his successor, David Shinn. Shinn’s deputy director, Frank Strada, oversaw those three executions in which medical technicians struggled to insert catheters into the arms of condemned prisoners.
Strada left Arizona to become director of the Tennessee Department of Corrections. Pike’s was the second failed execution in Tennessee, and the first failed because they also couldn’t set lines in that prisoner’s arms. Strada resigned nearly a week ago.
Pike likely has a long road back to health.
Even if there was not enough pentobarbital in her bloodstream to kill her, 
“The whole body has been exposed to this serious blood flow,” Zivot said. “If it affects the brain, it could affect the kidneys, the liver, the intestines, the lungs — all of it. I think it will be revealed soon enough.”
Corinna Lain, a University of Virginia Law professor who has extensively researched lethal injection, suggested that perhaps the secret was in knowing how to push the drugs.
Zivot, the anesthesiologist, discounted that theory and questioned whether the secret lay in the preparation of the raw pentobarbital salts into an injectable liquid form, “some way of adjusting the pH so it’s not quite so alkaline.”
But Michaela Almgren, a professor of pharmacology at the University of South Carolina, says that there is little leeway there.
“The catch is that there is a specific pH range in which it has to stay to meet the drug quality,” she said. “We don’t really have clinical evidence, but we don’t study it.” 
There’s the rub.
What kind of doctor takes money to kill people?
“The medical scientists operate under the same Hippocratic oath as doctors,” Lain said.
“We’re experts in non-killing,” Zivot said. “Anesthesiologists know about drug toxicity and other things. These are dangerous substances, and when mishandled, they can cause dangerous outcomes. But it’s not the practice of medicine in any way.”
What kind of doctor takes money to kill people on behalf of the state, anyway?
“The state may want to use these people,” Zivot said, “but that’s clearly not medicine.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: John James introduces bill to use tariff revenue for manufacturer relief
description: U.S. Rep. John James, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, introduced legislation in the U.S. House Tuesday to use tariff revenues to help American manufacturers harmed by the increased costs and supply chain disruptions stemming from tariffs levied by the Trump administration on other countries and retaliatory tariffs imposed on the United States. “Michiga[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. John James, R-Shelby Twp., speaks to reporters at the Michigan Capitol in Lansing, Mich., after Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's eighth and final State of the State address on Feb. 25, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)U.S. Rep. John James, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, introduced legislation in the U.S. House Tuesday to use tariff revenues to help American manufacturers harmed by the increased costs and supply chain disruptions stemming from tariffs levied by the Trump administration on other countries and retaliatory tariffs imposed on the United States.
“Michigan is disproportionally affected by the trade war, so it’s reasonable to use tariff revenue to reduce the effect on Michigan businesses and workers,” the Shelby Township Republican said in a press release from his office. “Our country needs to push back on unfair trade practices, but states like Michigan should not have to shoulder that burden alone.”
According to the text of the bill, H.R. 10759, to receive assistance, applicants must conduct “substantial production, manufacturing, agricultural, processing, or related productive activity in the United States,” and must meet a number of requirements around keeping production and manufacturing activity within the United States.
The legislation would establish several types of aid, including a refundable tariff impact credit, tariff working-capital loans for those “experiencing short-term liquidity constraints,” and rapid relief for “critical employers” in the case of imminent risk of closure of a domestic manufacturing facility or substantial layoffs. 
U.S. Customs station at the Blue Water Bridge in Port Huron, Michigan. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)
It would also establish an “American investment credit” to fund actions to expand or establish domestic production, reshore supply chains, or substitute U.S.-made products for tariff-affected foreign inputs.
At least 35% of the assistance would be required to go to small or midsize businesses, meaning those up to twice the industry size standard set by the Small Business Act. 
The relief would be financed through the “Tariff Relief for American Development and Employment Fund” or “TRADE Fund,” using “net additional customs duties attributable to covered tariff actions, after refunds, drawbacks, and administrative adjustments.”
Tariffs have been a top concern for voters in Michigan and across the country as affordability becomes a central issue ahead of the November general election. James’ Democratic gubernatorial competitor, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, has attacked James repeatedly for supporting GOP leadership in levying the tariffs. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Michigan Smart Trade Alliance is tracking an estimate of the financial impact of tariffs under the Trump administration on Michigan households. The tracker, as of Oct. 9, shows a statewide tariff impact of more than $27.2 billion in Michigan since January 2025, or about $6,667 per household.
“The costs on Michigan families is taking a toll in the form of higher costs and frustration with trade policies and tariffs that are holding our economy back,” Michigan Smart Trade Alliance spokesperson John Sellek said when the tariff tracker was announced. “It’s time to end the trade war with Canada, get both sides to the negotiation table, and find a solution that will end this affordability crisis in Michigan.”
In Michigan, tariffs against Canada — and those levied in retaliation by the Canadian government — have been especially prominent due to the state’s proximity to Canada and a historically strong trade relationship between Michigan and its neighbor to the north.
For example, disputes over tariffs delayed the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge between Detroit and Windsor, Ont., and conversations escalated to the point that Canadian leaders hosted a grand opening celebration without any American officials present. 
The Gordie Howe International Bridge, seen from Windsor, Ontario. July 24, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
“I fought with Canadians in Iraq. We have a deep and abiding bond that will not extinguish. I’m committed to making sure we continue to improve and deepen our relationships, and making sure our differences are resolved in a civil manner, quickly,” James said. “Our countries need to work out a reciprocal, fair, and mutually beneficial arrangement so we can bring back jobs and protect our industry.”
The House is not expected to hold any votes until after the November general election, and the current legislative session ends in late 2026. However, Congress is expected to return to Washington after the election for a lame duck session that will include voting on appropriations bills for 2027, as funding expires in mid-December under the current funding package.
James referenced the bill in both a Tuesday debate with Benson and in a conversation at the Detroit Economic Club in September, though details of the bill were only just made available Friday.
The bill has been referred to the House committees on Financial Services and Ways and Means.
Michigan Democrats criticized the timing of the legislation — Michigan Democratic Party spokesperson Derrick Honeyman called the bill “nothing but a desperate political stunt from a flailing D.C. politician,” citing the fact that Congress is out of session until after the election. 
And a spokesperson for Benson’s gubernatorial campaign similarly called the bill “a last minute political stunt designed to distract from his record of making life more expensive.”
“The timing tells you everything. After voting to continue Trump’s tariffs and getting called out for the $6,400 John James Tax he saddled on Michiganders’ backs, John James introduced this bill only after the House had ended its session and sent members home. If he was serious about passing this legislation he would’ve introduced it when the House was in session and secured even one cosponsor for it,” Benson’s press secretary Rajan Srinivasan said.

title: Trump appoints committee to revive quest to remove Lisa Cook from Fed board
text: President Donald Trump has formed a White House committee to investigate Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, escalating even further a lengthy feud with the Federal Reserve Board member.The three-member committee will seek evidence that Cook made false statements in obtaining a mortgage and will hold a closed-door hearing at the White House on Nov. 5, two days after the midterm elections, according to a presidential memorandum. The memorandum is dated Oct. 7 but was published to the White House website Friday.Trump tried to fire Cook last year after Bill Pulte, then the director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, alleged she lied on a mortgage form to obtain a more favorable rate. A U.S. Supreme Court decision in June found Trump did not have cause to remove Cook from the independent board. The president tasked the committee with finding enough evidence of wrongdoing to meet the court’s standard for firing. “As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote.Attorneys for Cook said Trump’s record of trying to fire Cook raised major concerns that the process would be illegitimate.The committee will be composed of Assistant to the President for Economic Policy Kevin Hassett, Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Chair Andrea Lucas and acting Director of the U.S. Office of Government Ethics Keith Sonderling. They are permitted to “consult with appropriate personnel from executive branch departments and agencies, including the Department of Justice.”The memorandum calls for Cook to be present for questioning at the Nov. 5 hearing. She is also permitted to submit a written statement to the committee. The memorandum also calls for Cook to comply with the committee’s requests for documents or other evidentiary material.Cook can also submit another written statement up to five days after the hearing.The committee will then write its own report with a recommendation to Trump on “whether there is cause to remove Governor Cook.” Cook’s attorneys Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen said in a statement that an objective investigation would show no wrongdoing, and that Cook looked forward to clearing her name.“In light of the President’s repeated statements that he has already decided to fire Governor Cook – regardless of the facts and evidence -  we have grave doubts that this ‘hearing’ is a legitimate one that would conform to the law,” they wrote. “But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board.” Trump has squabbled with Cook and former Fed Chair Jerome Powell, whom he appointed and who still serves on the board, over interest rates that the president believes should be lower to stimulate the economy. He has used legal investigations to pressure Cook and Powell, including a probe into Powell’s oversight of a Fed headquarters renovation.

name: National
title: Measles cases reach 4,080 for the year — the highest in decades
description: Measles cases for the calendar year surpassed 4,000 for the first time in decades, with as many as five deaths in Pennsylvania, as the federal government steps in with financial help for states but also fans vaccination fears and skepticism.  A weekly report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showed 4,080 cases this […]
text:
A sign at a University of Utah health clinic warns visitors about the spread of measles. The state has had 535 reported cases this year, among the largest counts in the country. (Photo by McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)Measles cases for the calendar year surpassed 4,000 for the first time in decades, with as many as five deaths in Pennsylvania, as the federal government steps in with financial help for states but also fans vaccination fears and skepticism. 
A weekly report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showed 4,080 cases this year as of Oct. 8, up 192 cases in a week. 
Pennsylvania, which has reported five confirmed deaths from measles, alone had 142 new cases for the week — for a total of 1,105 for the year. The CDC has recognized just two of the state’s reported deaths.
Measles cases have reached a 35-year high

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, has protested the CDC’s death count; his state’s five deaths would be more than the three deaths reported in 2025 for the entire nation.   
Other states with large numbers of cases, more than 200, did not see their case numbers change for the week: South Carolina (670 for the year), Utah (535) and Wisconsin (207). States with more cases included New York, which declared a measles emergency, with 19 new cases for a total of 103 this year; and Iowa, up 17 cases to 39. 
Kentucky reported separately on Friday that cases there had reached 104, up 10 from last week. 
Pennsylvania, which has become ground zero for this year’s outbreaks, reported this week that a new awareness and pop-up vaccine clinics are leading to more measles vaccinations.   
All but five states have had at least one measles case this year. The last time the United States had this many cases was in 1991, reaching 9,643 cases as the nation still struggled to roll out vaccinations for the disease, amid budget cuts that hit programs in big cities. 
Pennsylvania’s health department this week announced “a surge of interest” in vaccinations as more residents become aware of the outbreak — more than 56,000 doses were given out in September, more than twice the usual monthly volume. The state has added pop-up clinics in the most affected areas.  All but four of the measles cases were among unvaccinated people. 
The Lewistown Sentinel reported that an 18-year-old woman there died in September from brain swelling as a result of the measles virus after two of her brothers survived the disease. 
While the federal government has offered states more funding to combat measles, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy moved forward this week on plans to emphasize vaccine injury, announcing a new clinic and work to strengthen a database that tracks problems after a vaccination. 
“We must listen to patients and families who report vaccine injuries — not dismiss or gaslight them,” Kennedy said in a statement. 
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Roger Marshall’s complicated history of blurring the line between taxpayer dollars and campaign cash
description: Editor’s note: This story is a collaboration between Kansas Reflector and MS NOW. As Sen. Roger Marshall fights for his political life in Kansas, a staffer for Democrat Adam Hamilton — Marshall’s opponent — has been needling the Republican senator’s staff with an unusual question: Are any of you getting paid? According to Marshall’s most […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall appears at the Sept. 12, 2026, debate at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)Editor’s note: This story is a collaboration between Kansas Reflector and MS NOW.
As Sen. Roger Marshall fights for his political life in Kansas, a staffer for Democrat Adam Hamilton — Marshall’s opponent — has been needling the Republican senator’s staff with an unusual question: Are any of you getting paid?
According to Marshall’s most recent Federal Election Commission records filed in July, no one working for Marshall’s campaign had received a paycheck in the past five years — a situation that campaign finance experts said was potentially unprecedented in the modern era of politics.
But according to Marshall’s chief of staff, Brent Robertson, the campaign now does have some paid staff, though he declined to offer evidence or details, such as how many people were being paid or when their employment began.
Still, campaign experts say the situation raises questions about the line between Marshall’s campaign and his taxpayer-funded Senate office. 
In a joint investigation, Kansas Reflector and MS NOW obtained audio recordings, photos, videos, screenshots of text messages and calendar items from 2020 — when Marshall first ran for his Senate seat — that appear to show the senator and his top aide repeatedly using congressional staff and government resources in ways that experts say likely crossed the line between official business and campaigning.
According to the Members’ Congressional Handbook, if the “primary purpose” of a trip is for a non-official event or purpose, “the office cannot schedule official activities around the non-official event/purpose to make the travel eligible for congressional offices to be reimbursed.”
But the materials obtained by Kansas Reflector and MS NOW show the office repeatedly testing that principle during Marshall’s 2020 campaign — and multiple former staffers recounted instances when the office seemed to function more as a campaign arm than a taxpayer-funded Senate office. 
After promising to “meaningfully” respond to a detailed list of questions if Kansas Reflector and MS NOW extended its deadline for comment, Ryan Dollar, a lawyer for the Marshall campaign, sent a statement that did not address the questions.
“The Marshall campaign will not share, nor has any obligation to share campaign operations information with our opponent’s reporters, and Kansans know that Senator Marshall and his team fully comply with both FEC rules and Senate ethics while fighting for Kansas,” Dollar wrote, claiming the story came from “a disgruntled employee.”
There are real questions, however, whether Marshall and his team have fully complied with all FEC and congressional ethics rules.
At one point in the more than 200 texts reviewed, Robertson successfully arranges a single official meeting in Chicago and then instructs staff that the entire campaign trip would now be deemed “Official,” allowing them to book flights for Marshall using taxpayer funds.
According to the 2020 calendar items, many of the trips Marshall expensed to his Members’ Representational Allowance — the taxpayer-funded account used to operate congressional offices — included campaign events. The staff had a color-coded system to delineate what was an official meeting and what was campaign-related.
During one trip to Oklahoma at the end of September 2020, according to notes one former staffer took, Marshall used his leadership PAC to pay for his flights. Robertson, however, booked hotels and paid for restaurant meals with the MRA. 
A trip to Dallas the next month, in October 2020, warranted Marshall using campaign funds to book flights, according to the notes. But he used taxpayer dollars for a meal, despite the only official event on his calendar being a Zoom meeting. In contrast, a screenshot of his color-coded calendar shows his attendance at a Cowboys v. Giants game, three meetings and a fundraising dinner all marked as political events.
When staff objected at one point to booking what appeared to be a campaign trip using official government funds, Robertson told them they could blame him if they were ever deposed, according to a text message a former staffer sent their mother at the time.
During one text exchange, after Robertson was asked whether the primary purpose of a trip was official or campaign, the chief of staff wrote: “Primary purpose is what we say it is.”
During another exchange, a staffer asked for more details about a dinner at a steakhouse in Dodge City, Kansas. 
“Was any other staff eating at the Prime on Nine? They’re questioning the $170 price tag for 2,” the staffer asked Robertson.
“Who is they,” Robertson asked. He ultimately declared “there’s no statutory limit on what I can spend on meals.”
“Approve it,” he wrote.
Experts noted there is a statutory limit on what government employees can spend on food, and it is “not to exceed the daily rate for meals” that is established yearly by the General Services Administration. For Kansas in 2020, it was $55.
In another text exchange, Robertson claims he got clarification that the office only needs one official meeting to allow it to use taxpayer funds to travel for a slate of campaign events.
“We have a lot more leash than even I thought. Go ahead and book Philly for Doc,” Robertson wrote about a March 2020 trip to Philadelphia for Marshall, whom staffers refer to as “Doc.” “There is no ratio system at all.”
“Will literally need one official meeting per trip,” Robertson wrote.
Campaign finance experts disputed Robertson’s interpretation.
Craig Holman, a campaign finance and government ethics expert at Public Citizen — a nonprofit consumer rights and good government group founded by Ralph Nader — said these accounts of Marshall and his office’s “blatant disregard” for congressional ethics rules are “both breathtaking and seemingly very damning of Marshall’s character.”
“Not only do many of the travel events strongly suggest deliberate violations of the law, but even off-the-cuff remarks by staff show an intentionality of these infractions and efforts to cover them up from public view,” Holman said.
“Federal law and congressional ethics rules are very clear that government resources pay for official travel related to congressional duties, and campaign funds and personal budgets must be used to pay for the campaign or personal components of congressional travel,” Holman said, adding that Marshall appears to have used taxpayer dollars for “all aspects of campaign trips and personal travel.”
Brett Kappel, a lawyer at Harmon Curran who’s an authority on campaign finance, said contrary to Robertson’s assertion, “staff do not, actually, have a long leash” on the use of official funds for campaign purposes.
“There are a few, very limited, and very specific exceptions that permit the use of official resources for campaign purposes,” Kappel said, quoting a House Ethics memo on campaign activity.
The text messages also reference Marshall’s transportation to Florida, where his house in Sarasota has become a campaign issue.
At one point in the texts, Robertson instructs staff to fly Marshall “from Kansas to Sarasota as a stopover in the future.”
Where Marshall primarily lives has become an issue in his re-election campaign. During a debate last month at the Kansas State Fair, as Marshall talked about his $1.2 million Florida home, a combative crowd chanted, “You don’t live here!”
The texts show staff repeatedly navigating Marshall’s unique travel demands. The Kansas City Star reported in August that Marshall took at least 14 official trips through Sarasota between 2021 and 2024, costing taxpayers $18,886, according to the Star’s analysis of travel expenses reported by Marshall’s office to the Secretary of the Senate.
Marshall’s office told MS NOW on Thursday for a separate story that Marshall had sold his Florida home. As of Friday, the Zillow listing for the house, which had a list price of $1.45 million, said “accepting backups.”
Robertson has also been the subject of his own commuting controversy. A Politico investigation last year reported that he charged taxpayers $44,000 over the course of two years for expenses related to commuting from his home in Lynchburg, Virginia, to his workplace in Washington, D.C. Public records show the total is now more than $71,000.
Stanley Brand, an attorney who served as House general counsel under Speaker Tip O’Neill, told Politico he had “never” heard of a similar arrangement, though Marshall’s office said the expensing was “in full accordance and approval of Senate ethics, rules, and guidelines.”
A 2020 meeting Kansas Reflector and MS NOW were able to review, however, offered an example of Marshall himself potentially violating those ethics, rules and guidelines.
 
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall appears at a Sept. 14, 2026, rally by Vice President JD Vance at Webco Manufacturing in Olathe. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Marshall’s ‘pep talk’
On Oct. 13, 2020, Marshall texted senior staff on his official and campaign side to set up a “pep talk” with “everyone.”
“Yes everybody,” Marshall wrote.
Government ethics experts said that meeting appears to have violated federal ethics rules that prohibit the use of “official resources” for campaign purposes.
Both congressional and campaign staff — many using taxpayer-funded equipment like cellphones and computers — were summoned to the “MANDATORY ALL-STAFF CALL,” as it appeared in their official email calendars. And video of the Oct. 14, 2020, Zoom call shows Marshall and his congressional aides discussing the status of his campaign.
Throughout the call, Marshall talks about a campaign sign shortage and what door-knockers are hearing on the ground. He also asks his campaign manager for “talking points” and “helpful hints” for dealing with voters who were concerned about healthcare.
Some staff felt the Zoom call was such a clear-cut violation of ethics rules that they were compelled to document their concerns. 
“Sending this message as a reference that we objected to this illegal (activity) and that I raised it with our superiors and noted that it is not permissible per the above ethics statute,” Marshall’s legislative director at the time, Michael Brooks, texted another congressional staffer.
Brooks didn’t respond to inquiries for this story.
Holman said the Oct. 13 meeting “clearly crosses the line into illegal behavior.” 
“Members of Congress and all of their staff are thoroughly briefed against mixing office time and official resources with campaign duties,” he said. “All staff are given step-by-step instructions on how to honor the wall between official duties and campaign activities.” 
“That would be why Marshall’s staff was acutely aware that the staff ‘pep talk’ about the campaign on official time was not legally permissible,” Holman continued. “Both Marshall and the staff may be held liable for that violation.”
Marshall is currently in a close Senate race with Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton, who leads the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation. Recent polling has shown the race essentially tied, turning a reliably red Senate seat into a competitive contest. And while Hamilton’s campaign has outraised Marshall in donations, national Republicans are pouring money into Kansas to protect Marshall. No Democrat from Kansas has won a Senate seat since 1932.
Marshall has also faced intense scrutiny following a New York Times report about lawsuits filed against former patients over unpaid medical bills. His campaign has pushed back aggressively against the allegations, with a spokeswoman for Marshall saying he spent decades caring for patients regardless of their ability to pay.
“Judges issue warrants when people repeatedly miss court dates, not doctors,” Payton Fuller, the communications director for Marshall’s office, wrote in a statement.
But even that response underscores the unusual overlap between Marshall’s official office and his campaign: Fuller is both a current congressional staffer — earning a taxpayer-funded salary — and an unpaid campaign volunteer spokeswoman. For that separate story involving Marshall’s Florida property, MS NOW reached out to a generic press email for the campaign. Fuller wrote back, from her campaign email, as “communications director for Senator Roger Marshall.”
Amid Marshall’s close race, the idea that he wouldn’t have any paid staff gave government ethics and campaign finance experts pause.
One expert noted that Marshall had somehow been operating a campaign with surprisingly few expenses. According to his FEC reports, Marshall only spent $206,869 on his campaign from the beginning of 2025 until August — the last reporting period.
“For a Senate campaign, it is extremely uncommon for there not to be expenses for campaign staff and countless other normal campaign expenses,” said Kedric Payne, the vice president and general counsel of the Campaign Legal Center.
He added that senators may be subject to criminal penalties if they or anyone in their office misuses official funds with their knowledge. And if Marshall’s office “used taxpayer funds for campaign activity disguised as official business, it is a clear violation of one of the most basic ethics rules.”
“These very serious allegations warrant at the very least an immediate and credible explanation from the senator’s office,” Payne said. “Otherwise, a Senate Ethics Committee investigation is needed.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Criminalizing reproductive healthcare makes pregnancy more dangerous
description: For decades, anti-abortion extremists have mobilized at the national and state levels to strip away our bodily autonomy. That is why those of us in the reproductive justice movement have always said that Roe v. Wade was never enough to protect our communities.
text:
Clinic escorts attempt to stand between patients and anti-abortion protesters outside A Preferred Women’s Health Center of Atlanta in Forest Park, Georgia, in July 2023. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)Since the dismantling of Roe v. Wade, medication abortion has become one of the most common methods of managing miscarriages and ending pregnancies in the United States. Medication abortion is essential care, especially in states with abortion bans or restrictions. 
Despite abortion medication’s proven safety, lawmakers are aggressively working to restrict its distribution and even criminalize possession. 
Attacks on abortion care are not new. For decades, anti-abortion extremists have mobilized at the national and state levels to strip away our bodily autonomy. That is why those of us in the reproductive justice movement have always said that Roe v. Wade was never enough to protect our communities. 
It is time that we look beyond abortion access to laying the foundations for a future in which we can all not only have the right to decide if and when to have children, but also to know that if we do, that we will have equal access to the conditions that will allow us to care for our families in thriving communities. 
Reproductive justice asks us to imagine a world with economic stability, access to nutritious foods, clean air and water, quality housing and schools, and neighborhoods free from violence and exploitation.  
The overturning of Roe was just one step in a coordinated plan to dismantle reproductive healthcare. While Southern states have served as a testing ground for abortion restrictions and other limits to bodily autonomy for decades, this can no longer be written off as a Southern issue. 
Since the Dobbs decision, 23 states have banned or severely restricted abortion care. But the bans haven’t just prevented people from accessing abortion care, they’ve stood in the way of fertility care, miscarriage treatment, pregnancy care and assistive reproductive technologies like IVF.  
We know extremist lawmakers hellbent on controlling the bodies of others won’t stop there. 
Already, we’ve seen Louisiana reclassify mifepristone as a Schedule IV drug, criminalizing its possession and making it less accessible to physicians in emergency situations. While many view this as a major shift in our country’s history, reproductive justice leaders recognize this as just the latest strategy used to  reduce bodily autonomy, limit opportunity, maintain control of and finally imprison marginalized people — particularly Black people and people of color, poor folks, and LGBTQ+ communities.
In 2023, Louisiana had the highest maternal mortality rate in the country. Louisiana’s criminalization of mifepristone has since likely worsened maternal mortality and morbidity by causing delays in critical pregnancy care such as emergency postpartum hemorrhage management. The Schedule IV classification also requires increased licensing and reporting for the drugs, creating a chilling effect among medical and pharmacy professionals who fear surveillance and criminalization if they dispense the medications, even for uses not related to abortion care. 
By criminalizing abortion medication, legislators are making pregnancy and childbirth even more dangerous.
In 2022, Tennessee lawmakers passed a law that made it a Class E felony to provide abortion-inducing medication through courier delivery/mail services. Violators can face between one to six years in prison. 
At this moment, the rest of the country should look to the South to understand what is coming and to learn from its long history of resistance and building alternative systems of care to support their communities.
For many Black communities across the South, medication abortion is not just a matter of convenience, but it is often the most  accessible option. With many abortion clinics in the South forced to close following the end of Roe, medication abortion can create additional pathways to care — especially for rural communities who face increased transportation and economic barriers. These barriers are being exacerbated by the recent drastic funding cuts to Medicaid that put hundreds of rural hospitals at risk of closure. 
By imposing criminal penalties on medication abortion, states are further stripping our most vulnerable communities of their autonomy while also putting their lives at risk. More than a third of birthing people now live in a county or parish with no obstetric care — in an emergency that can very well make the difference between life and death.
A future where healthcare is rooted in autonomy, empowerment and equality is possible. Building that future requires meaningful and long-term engagement from communities, advocates and policymakers. 
Marginalized people have disproportionately had to navigate systems that control their bodies and deny them access to comprehensive care. Black women in the reproductive justice movement have been strategizing to meet this moment for decades, and they have the experience, expertise and vision needed to lead us toward that liberated future. 
Their voices and lived realities must be centered in present-day conversations to shape policies and systems of care that will move us toward greater reproductive freedom.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Beshear and Rogers announce federal funding projects for Eastern Kentucky revitalization
description: CORBIN, Ky. — While Republican U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers and Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear disagreed on how President Donald Trump’s policies are impacting Appalachian Kentucky, the two came together Friday to announce money going toward economic development in the region.  At the annual Shaping Our Appalachia Region Summit in Corbin, Rogers and Beshear announced[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers, left, and Gov. Andy Beshear, right, present  at the 2026 SOAR Summit in Corbin. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)CORBIN, Ky. — While Republican U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers and Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear disagreed on how President Donald Trump’s policies are impacting Appalachian Kentucky, the two came together Friday to announce money going toward economic development in the region. 
At the annual Shaping Our Appalachia Region Summit in Corbin, Rogers and Beshear announced $22 million federal funding to support various services in Eastern Kentucky, like healthcare, emergency services, infrastructure for economic development projects and more. 
Beshear said in his remarks that because of Trump’s “war choice in Iran and his foreign tariffs are causing prices to skyrocket.” The governor also emphasized his past criticism of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which he said would close rural hospitals and end coverage for 250,000 Kentuckians if federal Medicaid funding is cut. 
“I’m going to do everything I can to make sure we blunt that very difficult thing that’s headed our way,” Beshear told the crowd, which included state lawmakers, local government officials and more. 
Asked about Beshear’s comments afterwards, Rogers said “of course I stand with the president.”
“That’s the national government,” Rogers continued. “And I’ll let the governor deal with whatever he wants.” 
Rogers founded SOAR in 2013 with the current governor’s father, former Democratic Gov. Steve Beshear. In his speech, Rogers said Eastern Kentuckians have come together to find solutions to problems such as rebuilding after floods, a lack of jobs, bolstering education and providing better healthcare. 
“You are making a difference, and you offer great opportunities for people to come and live with us,” Rogers said. 
The $22 million announced Friday comes from the Abandoned Mine Lands Economic Revitalization (AMLER) program, which Rogers established in 2016. Those projects are: 

More than $4 million to the Leslie County Fiscal Court to install over 35,000 linear feet of gas line for existing and future businesses. 
$3.5 million to the City of London Convention and Tourism Commission in Laurel County for infrastructure for the Wilderness Road Event Center.
$2.9 million for Johnson County Schools to support the nursing and agriculture programs at the Johnson Central Career and Technical Center. 
$2.76 million to AdventHealth Manchester in Clay County for the hospital to purchase a DaVinci 5 Robotic Surgical System.
$2.5 million to the Elliott County Fiscal Court to replace the current emergency medical services facility in Sandy Hook with a larger, modernized structure. 
More than $2.2 million to the City of Cumberland in Harlan County to replace its aging water distribution infrastructure and add new water lines. 
$2.15 million to Letcher County Water and Sewer District (LCWSD) to install a new waterline and provide water services for the Mountain Comprehensive Health Corp.
$1.64 million to the City of Booneville in Owsley County for the Sag Hollow Business Development Phase II to expand overnight lodging at the Sag Hollow area through the construction of three executive cabins. 
$600,000 to the Pike County Fiscal Court to construct a build-ready pad at the Wolfpit Industrial Park.

Rogers and Beshear also highlighted $25.7 million to the Center for Rural Development for six projects to expand high speed internet access across a dozen counties. Beshear previously spoke about that funding on Wednesday during a press conference as part of $78.8 million awarded by the Appalachian Regional Commission to Kentucky in fiscal year 2026.

name: VTDigger
title: Police identify officer and victim involved in Williston shooting
description:
The officer, Ethan Favreau, has been placed on administrative leave. No charges have been filed as of Friday afternoon. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Police identify officer and victim involved in Williston shooting.
text:
Police tape showing a blurred scene with vehicles and lights in the distance. Photo via Adobe Stock
Vermont State Police have identified the people involved in Thursday’s police shooting in Williston. 

Officer Ethan Favreau joined the Williston Police Department in Sept. 2019, after having previously served with the Chittenden County Sheriff’s Office. Photo provided by Vermont State Police

Officer Ethan Favreau of the Williston Police Department shot and injured Michael McGovern, 52, of St. George, Thursday morning, a VSP press release Friday said. No charges have been filed, and no one is in custody. 
Vermont State Police’s initial investigation found that the shooting occurred around 4:50 a.m. along Route 2A where officers were responding to a road hazard. 
McGovern approached the hazard, but further details “remain under investigation,” Maj. Ashley Barnes, commander of the state police criminal division, told reporters at a press conference Thursday.
Both Favreau and McGovern were seen at the University of Vermont Medical Center in Burlington. McGovern was treated for a gunshot wound to the hip, and Favreau was “evaluated for a minor injury.” Both were discharged, a Thursday afternoon release said. 

READ MORE

Another Williston officer — who has not been identified — was on the scene, but did not fire a weapon. Favreau has been placed on paid administrative leave.

title: Election betting is booming as the midterms near. Do states have the power to curb it?
text: On Friday morning, the prediction market platform Kalshi gave the Democratic candidate in Minnesota’s U.S. Senate race an 87% chance of winning. The volume of trading on the outcome exceeded $1.8 million.This is exactly the type of activity Minnesota and numerous other states want to shut down.“They jeopardize people’s trust in government and government decision-making. They jeopardize people’s trust in elections,” said Minnesota state Rep. Emma Greenman, a member of the state’s Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party. She helped spearhead Minnesota’s first-in-the-nation near-total ban on prediction markets earlier this year.Prediction markets have emerged as a flashpoint in state and federal relations, as a host of states struggle with the Trump administration over who has authority to regulate the platforms and whether state laws restricting gambling apply to them. While much of the fight centers on the future of sports betting, a growing number of state officials fear the sites are opening the door to a new era of gambling on elections — a practice many states have long prohibited.Some state election officials have warned their residents in recent months that using prediction markets to place money on elections is illegal. Others are locked in litigation with the platforms. At least one state, Arizona, has filed criminal charges against Kalshi.But the prediction markets remain widely available as Election Day approaches, with the industry maintaining that the federal government has authority over the platforms, not the states.Betting on control of CongressOn the two leading prediction market sites, Kalshi and Polymarket, individuals can put money down on the outcome of a wide array of races and related questions, like whether Kansas or Nebraska’s U.S. Senate races will have a larger margin of victory. That includes which party will control Congress following the midterm elections. On Friday morning, the Democratic Party had a 90% chance of winning the U.S. House on Polymarket.Money changing hands over the outcome of elections is corrosive to democracy and amounts to an attempt to bypass existing bans on election betting, civic organizations and some public officials say. Twenty-three states completely ban election betting, according to data from the National Conference of State Legislatures analyzed by the Pew Research Center.“It’s supposed to be a civic duty where people are deciding what candidate they actually think is best for a leadership position, not what candidate can make them the most money if they bet the right way,” said Benjamin Schiffrin, director of securities policy at Better Markets, a nonprofit watchdog group advocating for consumer and investor financial protections.The prediction markets and their supporters say the sites offer contracts that pay out if a given event or outcome occurs. Under that view, the contracts are essentially swaps, a financial product often traded by sophisticated investors to hedge against economic risk. Critics of the platforms say the contracts effectively function as wagers. Unlike swaps, which investors use to help offset the effects of events like rising interest rates, contracts on sporting events, elections and other non-financial questions serve no legitimate hedging purpose, they say.CFTC and prediction marketsThe Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal regulator that oversees markets for swaps, has asserted authority to regulate the platforms.In a statement, Polymarket said it maintains that “prediction markets are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission under a federal framework, not a patchwork of state rules."Kalshi didn’t respond to a request for comment. In a March court filing in a federal lawsuit, lawyers for Kalshi wrote that its events contracts are swaps and that election and sports contracts “fit comfortably” within that definition.“The outcomes of political events such as elections are connected to obvious financial consequences,” the court filing says.The Trump administration has firmly sided with the prediction markets. The CFTC is made up of five members, but currently only has a single commissioner, Michael Selig, who was appointed by President Donald Trump in 2025.Selig has taken a favorable stance toward the industry, and in June the CFTC proposed a rule that would set up a new framework for how the commission regulates events contracts. The rule would continue to allow trading on elections.In a July 27 letter to the CFTC, 16 civic watchdog groups, including Better Markets, Common Cause and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, warned that the rule ignores concerns about the harm the contracts could cause to elections.“Event contracts that involve elections allow individuals to bet on elections, which is illegal under many state laws. This election betting would incentivize election interference and has the potential to undermine the integrity of our democracy,” the groups wrote, urging the commission to prohibit election-related events contracts because they go against the public interest.The CFTC didn’t respond to questions from States Newsroom.“Congress gave the @CFTC the exclusive authority to regulate prediction markets,” Selig wrote on social media in August. He added that the commission would defend its jurisdiction against states “seeking to nullify federal law and apply state anti-gaming laws” to the platforms.Maryland issues public warningIn Maryland, Jared DeMarinis, the state administrator of elections, said that in his view, the election contracts on prediction markets violate the plain meaning of his state’s prohibition on election gambling. The Maryland State Board of Elections, which oversees an office run by DeMarinis, issued a public warning about betting on elections in March and said that even though prediction market sites are accessible to residents, the activity on them may still conflict with state law.DeMarinis argued that it’s important to take a strong position against election betting while the prediction market industry remains in its infancy. By 2028, a presidential election year, he fears betting on elections could become a more firmly entrenched practice.“This is kind of like a watershed moment. You can kind of end it before it proliferates,” DeMarinis said. DeMarinis in July asked the Maryland Office of the State Prosecutor, which investigates violations of state election law, to examine the legality of election-related wagering on the platforms. Maryland State Prosecutor Charlton Howard wrote in an email that the agency doesn’t comment on the existence or status of an investigation unless it results in criminal charges.Wisconsin advisory, Arizona criminal chargesIn Wisconsin, the state Elections Commission issued a public advisory in July warning voters against gambling on elections, including on Kalshi and Polymarket. The commission cautioned that residents who bet on an election and then vote in the contest could have their ability to vote challenged in the future.The Wisconsin Elections Commission declined to make its administrator, Meagan Wolfe, available for an interview. But in a statement in July, Wolfe said that “it’s important for voters to understand the consequences if they bet on an election outcome.”Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes, a Democrat, filed state criminal charges against Kalshi in March. Mayes alleged the company had accepted bets from Arizona residents in violation of state law, including on sports and election wagering related to the 2028 presidential race, along with state-level contests in Arizona in 2026.Kalshi preemptively sued over the prosecution in federal court and obtained an order halting the case from U.S. District Court Judge Michael T. Liburdi, a Trump appointee. He ruled that Kalshi was likely to show that a federal law granting the CFTC the authority to regulate swaps preempted Arizona’s gambling laws.Liburdi wrote in his order that the CFTC had consistently treated weather-based financial products as swaps because weather events produce commercial consequences for a wide range of market participants. Contracts based on sports and elections function the same way, the judge wrote.“That these event contracts can be used to offset financial exposure confirms the association between the event and commercial consequences to stakeholders,” Liburdi wrote.Battles in the courtsThe fight over who has power over prediction markets — and therefore, potentially, election contracts — is unlikely to be settled until the U.S. Supreme Court takes action.The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, which covers much of the western United States, and the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals, which covers Delaware, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, have issued contradictory decisions. The 9th Circuit has sided with the states, finding that federal law doesn’t preempt state-level gambling restrictions, while the 3rd Circuit upheld the CFTC’s exclusive power to regulate events contracts.In September, New Jersey filed a petition asking the Supreme Court to decide whether federal law preempts states from regulating sports bets offered on markets registered with the CFTC — in other words, the prediction markets. The justices haven’t decided whether to take the case, but the high court is generally seen as more likely to intervene when lower courts are divided.New Jersey’s petition is framed around the uncertainty over sports betting, but the outcome could provide clarity on election contracts as well. In 2024 the CFTC attempted to block Kalshi from offering contracts about which party would control Congress, but an appeals court in the final weeks before Election Day allowed the company to continue.Schiffrin said the election contracts are essentially the same as the sports contracts. “You’re betting on the outcome of a contest. It should be considered gambling, no different than if you’re betting on the outcome of a sporting event,” he said.In Minnesota, a federal judge halted the state’s ban on prediction markets before it took effect this summer after the CFTC, Kalshi and Polymarket sued the state. U.S. District Court Judge Katherine Menendez, an appointee of President Joe Biden, ruled that federal law likely preempts the state’s ban on many contracts offered on prediction markets.Minnesota bans gambling on elections and hasn’t legalized sports betting. Greenman, the Minnesota state lawmaker, said decisions about whether to allow betting should be made by people in the state.“We should be rebuilding trust in government decision-making, that the public’s heart — the public’s interest — are what sit at the center,” Greenman said.

title: Nell Grace helps revitalize Jackson’s once-thriving Farish Street District
description: A photograph of Eunella "Nell" Rowe is displayed in the dining room of Nell Grace, a restaurant named for her and granddaughter Grace Rowe, on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Jackson's historic Farish Street District.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Stepping into Nell Grace is less like walking into a restaurant and more like melting into the soft, unhurried warmth of Big Mama’s embrace.
The restaurant is a hidden gem located at 111 East Church St., in downtown Jackson’s historic Farish Street District. And it is the vision of a father and son, Marc and Devan Rowe, who opened Nell Grace in January. 
Marc Rowe, left, with daughter Grace and son Devan at Nell Grace, the restaurant the father and son own and operate in Jackson’s historic Farish District, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Marc’s mother Eunella “Nell” Rowe is pictured in the background. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Marc Rowe named the eatery in honor of his mother, Eunella “Nell” Rowe, and his daughter, Grace.
“Naming the restaurant was my way of preserving my mother’s legacy,” Marc said, his voice filled with deep admiration and reverence. “I wanted her name to live on through something that brings people together. When guests come through our doors, share a meal and feel at home, that reflects the kind of spirit she had.”
Marc moves with a determined grace, disappearing into the buzz of the kitchen to check on meal preps before emerging to visit individual tables, smiling, chatting, asking diners if they are enjoying their meals. In one section, a large group celebrating a family member’s birthday sat before a floor-to-ceiling mural of a woman frozen in song, an artistic heartbeat for the room. 
Customers dine, chat and listen to music at Nell Grace restaurant in Jackson’s historic Farish Street District, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
On alternating nights, the air is filled with haunting melodies from violinist Daniel Parker and the sultry, late-night smoothness of saxophonist Keith Ward.
“A lot of what people see in me today came from her,” Devan said, reflecting on the deep influence of his grandmother. “She just had this way about her. She connected with people, and she had such a natural gift for making everyone feel comfortable, special and welcome.”
He said watching her taught him how much relationships matter. “The confidence, the way I connect with people, she planted those seeds in me a long time ago.”
Violinist Daniel Parker entertains diners at Nell Grace, a restaurant in Jackson’s historic Farish Street District, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Nell Grace has a laid-back, cozy vibe, with customers cradling cocktails while music drifts over tables and soothing aromas waft from the kitchen. Chatter and laughter subside as forks dig into savory Catfish Atchafalaya, steaks, blackened seafood and ribbons of Cajun pasta. 
Order up a burger or a variety of shrimp dishes, traditional wings or Cajun loaded fries. Down-home southern side dishes offer a familiar taste of home cooking — bubbling, baked macaroni and cheese, earthy black-eyed peas, golden cornbread, braised southern greens and sweet yams.
As the night deepens, the Rowes encourage diners to make room for warm peach cobbler, New Orleans-style beignets dusted in a snowfall of powdered sugar, delectable cheesecake or the richness of red velvet cake.
Saxophonist Keith Ward sings “Happy Birthday” to 1-year-old Janiya Winn at Nell Grace, a restaurant in Jackson’s historic Farish Street District, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“I spent more than 20 years in Atlanta working in entertainment, but something kept pulling me back home,” Devan Rowe said. “I felt like I had learned enough to bring something back home… learned to bring something meaningful back to Jackson.”
Together, the duo is dreaming a renaissance into existence, with plans to revitalize several historic properties in the Farish Street neighborhood, once the bustling hub of Jackson’s Black-owned businesses. Their vision weaves a tapestry of live entertainment, fine dining and cultural pilgrimages to create a destination that celebrates the district’s landmarks.
Catfish dinner with sides at Nell Grace restaurant in Jackson’s historic Farish Street District, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026.Nell Grace restaurant customer Jaylin Williams, left, offers saxophonist Keith Ward a dap of approval Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Jackson.A photograph of Eunella “Nell” Rowe is displayed on a wall at Nell Grace, the restaurant named for her and granddaughter Grace Rowe, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Jackson.Mixologist Megan Gibbs prepares cocktails for a customer at Nell Grace restaurant in Jackson’s historic Farish Street District, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026.A cocktail at Nell Grace restaurant in Jackson’s historic Farish Street District, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026.Strawberry daiquiris at Nell Grace restaurant in Jackson’s historic Farish Street District, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026.Nell Grace restaurant at 111 East Church St. in Jackson’s historic Farish Street District.Violinist Daniel Parker entertains diners at Nell Grace, a restaurant in Jackson’s historic Farish Street District, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026. The floor-to-ceiling mural is titled “Blue Lady,” painted by Jason Cooper.Justin Winn holds his 1-year-old daughter, Janiya, during a family dinner at Nell Grace restaurant in Jackson’s historic Farish Street District, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026.Saxophonist Keith Ward entertains diners at Nell Grace restaurant in Jackson’s historic Farish Street District, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026.
Devan said his father spent 26 years in child nutrition and the food industry.
“He understood the food and operations side, and I come from the entertainment side,” the son said. “I understood how to create an experience. Nell Grace is where those two worlds come together. To me, it is more than a name. When people walk in, I want them to feel like they’ve stepped into my grandmother’s hugs and welcoming home, not a restaurant.”
